## E60. [low] (cfs-detector-fixtures, confirmed) A GEQ band is a brick wall exactly three RTA bands wide: every RTA band receives the full gain of its log-nearest 1/3-octave band, and the ring sits exactly on an RTA centre, so RTA->GEQ mapping and cut depth are exact.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1129-1134 (_refresh_cuts: nearest GEQ band, full gains[k]+master applied as attenuation), src/x32mcp/meters.py:661-667 (set_geq_gain: full gain to RTA bands within +-1/6 oct), tests/test_meters.py:442-449, tests/integration/test_cfs.py:262-275 (2400 Hz ring -> band 69/70 -> GEQ 22, 'l2 < l1 - 3').

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/detector.py:538-543 (band_for_freq from the RTA band CENTRE, det.freq_hz = band_hz[band] at :316,422), :556-565 (merge_adjacent then keeps deepening whichever neighbour was opened first), src/x32mcp/cfs.py:1200-1219 (VERIFY failure => deepen same band to -9 then ABORT).

**Reality:** HANDOVER §4b#4: on the real desk a -15 dB GEQ cut (PRE) moved the RTA bands by only -5.9/-6.0/-3.9 dB - the analyser sees ~40% of the set cut on broadband content, and unevenly across the three bands; a 1/3-octave graphic band is a bell whose edge (+-1/6 oct) response is roughly half the centre setting, GEQ2 (non-TrueEQ) bands interact; a ring can sit anywhere inside a 1/10-oct RTA band (+-3.5%), so at the 2 k/2.5 k boundary (2236 Hz) RTA band 68 (2176 Hz +-76 Hz) maps to either GEQ band.

**On a real desk:** Ring at ~2.25 kHz: CFS opens GEQ 2 kHz, the ring gets ~-1.5 dB of a -3 dB cut; if that is not enough VERIFY fails and CFS deepens 2 kHz to -6/-9 (merge_adjacent also steers the next, correctly-mapped detection into the same wrong band) and may ABORT 'not tamed' with 9 dB cut beside the ring. The fake can never show this because its mapping and the controller's mapping are the same function.

**Offline test:** Replace FakeDesk._refresh_cuts' step function with a bell per GEQ band (e.g. RBJ peaking, Q~4.3, summed in dB across bands, evaluated at each RTA centre and at the injected ring's exact hz for the loop term); inject rings at 2176, 2236 and 2290 Hz and assert ring_out tames each within 2 notches on bands {21,22}; add a controller rule: on VERIFY failure at a boundary frequency try the other neighbour before deepening.

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (medium)** — All citations check out and there is no fallback the claimant missed.

Encoded assumption (verified): FakeDesk._refresh_cuts (src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1129-1134) maps every RTA band centre to its log-nearest GEQ band and applies that band's full gain (+master) as the RTA attenuation — a 3-band-wide brick wall. SyntheticRta.set_geq_gain (src/x32mcp/meters.py:661-667) does the same (full gain to every RTA band within ±1/6 oct). The synthetic ring's loop term uses the cut at the ring's RTA band index, not at its exact Hz (meters.py:716-717 `cut = self._cuts.get(r.band)`), so a ring anywhere inside an RTA band always receives 100% of whatever GEQ band the RTA-centre maps to. tests/test_meters.py:442-449 asserts exactly this (2500 Hz −3 dB → cuts {69:3,70:3,71:3}, ring at 2400 decays 2.25 dB/frame) and tests/integration/test_cfs.py:262-277 certifies the closed loop (2400 Hz ring → rta_band 69 → GEQ_BAND_2K5, `l2 < l1 - 3.0`).

Code dependency (verified): detector reports det.freq_hz = band_hz[band] (detector.py:316, Detection built at ~:418-427); NotchController.band_for_freq is the identical log-nearest mapping (detector.py:538-543); plan() (detector.py:552-565) deepens the nearest existing notch within merge_adjacent_bands (=1 by DESIGN.md:279) before opening the correct band; cfs._notch_and_verify (cfs.py:1200-1219) re-plans the same det on VERIFY failure, so it only ever deepens the same band (−3→−6→−9, DESIGN.md:276-277) and when plan() returns None it returns False → ring_out sets abort_reason 'ring at … not tamed' (cfs.py:1160-1162). No code path tries the other neighbouring GEQ band. Because the fake's RTA→GEQ map and the controller's freq→GEQ map are literally the same nearest-log function over the same RTA centres, the emulator can never produce a ring that the controller's chosen band under-cuts — the tests are self-confirming.

Reality (verified): HANDOVER §4b item 4 records that a −15 dB GEQ cut inserted PRE moved the three RTA bands by only −5.9/−6.0/−3.9 dB — partial and uneven, contradicting the fake's 'full cut on exactly 3 bands'. Physically a 1/3-octave graphic band is a bell (roughly half the dB at ±1/6 oct; GEQ/GEQ2 non-TrueEQ bands interact), and a ring can sit anywhere in a 1/10-oct RTA band, so at the 2k/2.5k geometric boundary (2236 Hz, inside RTA band 68 = 2102–2253 Hz) the ring gets ~half of either band's cut. docs/research say nothing about filter shape (only the ISO centre list, fx_routing_scenes.md §2.3), so nothing in the verified research licenses the brick-wall model.

Caveats (do not overturn the finding): the '40%' figure is the claimant's reading of one noisy music-background measurement, and CFS's VERIFY watches ring decay rather than measured cut depth (HANDOVER notes the ring stops acoustically wherever the RTA taps), so RTA-visible depth per se is not what CFS acts on. Also, feedback near onset usually has small excess loop gain (ring-out step_db default 1.0, DESIGN.md:284), so a half-strength −3 dB cut will often still tame a boundary ring; the ABORT-with-−9-dB-beside-the-ring outcome is plausible mainly in WATCH mode or with larger excess gain. The more common real cost is over-deep/misplaced cuts and merge_adjacent steering a correctly-mapped follow-up detection into the first (wrong) band. That is 'tool writes suboptimal state / can fail spuriously at a gig' — medium, as claimed; master is backed off on ABORT so it is not a safety issue.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The assumption is real but its consequence is overstated and largely mitigated.

TRUE PART: FakeDesk._refresh_cuts (src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1129-1134) and SyntheticRta.set_geq_gain (src/x32mcp/meters.py:661-667) model a 1/3-octave GEQ band as a brick wall: every RTA band takes the full gain of its log-nearest GEQ band and zero from any other, and the fake uses the same nearest-band function as NotchController.band_for_freq (detector.py:538-543), so mapping and cut depth are exact by construction. A real graphic-EQ band is a bell (RBJ/constant-Q, BW 1/3 oct: -3 dB centre -> -2.4 dB at 1/12 oct, -2.1 at 1/9, -1.5 at the +-1/6-oct edge, -0.6 at the neighbour's centre). docs/research says nothing about filter shape (only ISO centres, fx_routing_scenes.md §2.3), so physics is the reference. So yes: the emulator cannot exhibit partial-efficacy cuts, and no test can reveal that a boundary ring gets ~half the notch.

WHY IT DOES NOT BITE THE WAY CLAIMED:
1. The controller does not depend on exact cut depth. _notch_and_verify (cfs.py:1200-1219) treats every cut as uncertain: it measures the ring's decay (not the filter depth) and deepens -3 -> -6 -> -9. HANDOVER §4b#4 itself notes that when a notch breaks the loop the ring stops acoustically and the RTA sees that wherever it taps; the -15 -> -5.9/-6.0/-3.9 numbers are the analyser's view of broadband music through the filter (RTA skirt leakage + averaging + non-stationary content), not evidence that a cut delivers 40% at the ring frequency, and VERIFY never measures broadband filter depth.
2. In ring_out the loop-gain excess at onset is bounded by ringout.step_db = 1.0 dB (device.yaml:826). A -3 dB GEQ step gives >= 1.5 dB even at the exact band boundary, so the first notch brings loop gain below unity and VERIFY passes; the claimed 'deepen to -9 then ABORT with 9 dB beside the ring' needs > 4.5 dB of excess, which 1 dB raises cannot create. I simulated the finding's own proposed test (SyntheticRta ring at 2236 Hz, bell-model effective cut applied at the ring band): growth 15-20 dB/s (what every test uses, = 0.75-1 dB/frame excess) -> VERIFY PASS with one -3 notch at 1.5 dB effective (7 dB drop in 12-17 frames); 40 dB/s -> passes after one deepen (-6 -> -3 eff). Both satisfy the finding's 'tamed within 2 notches' criterion, i.e. the proposed offline test would NOT fail today.
3. 'Wrong band' at 2236-2253 Hz (RTA band 68 -> GEQ 2k though the ring is a hair closer to 2.5k) is a wash: at the geometric boundary both neighbours are equally (half-)effective, so mapping to either costs the same.
4. merge_adjacent deepening the first-opened neighbour (detector.py:556-565) is a deliberate budget-vs-depth design choice, and the brick-wall fake is PESSIMISTIC about it (deepening the neighbour does literally nothing to the ring in the fake, vs partial relief on a real bell), so tests are not hiding a rosier-than-real outcome there; plan() falls through to open the target band once the neighbour hits -9.
5. feedback_watch has no VERIFY at all (cfs.py:1040-1041: each re-detection after the 1 s cooldown just deepens), cuts-only, bounded at -9 by Policy - same physics a human faces with a 31-band GEQ.

WHAT REMAINS (real, low): boundary-frequency rings burn roughly 2x GEQ depth per dB of recovered headroom, so ring_out reaches the -9 dB ceiling and aborts 'not tamed' (orderly: backoff 6 dB, honest reason string at cfs.py:1161) after ~4.5 dB of extra gain at those frequencies instead of ~9 dB, and the controller never does what an engineer would (cut both adjacent bands for a boundary ring, or try the other neighbour before giving up). That is an efficiency/optimisation gap inherent to choosing a 1/3-oct GEQ, not a wrong write, not a safety issue, and not a tool reporting wrong state. Worth making the fake bell-shaped (sum of per-band peaking responses evaluated at each RTA centre and at the ring's exact Hz for the loop term) so such a both-neighbours rule could be developed offline, but severity is low, not medium.

## E61. [low] (cfs-detector-fixtures, partial) One clock: frame timestamps, cooldowns, VERIFY deadlines, dwell and report times all advance together and monotonically at 20 frames/s.

**Encoded at:** tests/test_detector.py:25,144 (ts = i*0.05 exactly), src/x32mcp/meters.py:582-583,725 (SyntheticRta virtual clock t0+i*period), in-memory loopback with zero jitter (tests/conftest.py); device.yaml:800 '40 frames = 2 s at 20 fps'.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/meters.py:392,457 (LiveMeters stamps frames with time.time() at receipt), src/x32mcp/cfs.py:1028-1029 (_consume silently drops any frame with ts <= last_ts), detector.py:431/304-310 (cooldown in frame-ts seconds) vs cfs.py:1228-1233 (VERIFY deadline on loop.time()) vs :1131 (dwell wall sleep) vs :493,979 (report clock time.time); frame-COUNT constants detector.py:100,117,123 (3/2/6 frames) assume 50 ms frames.

**Reality:** meters.md §1.2/§6.7: 50 ms is nominal, 'may be variable according to console's ability', DOC's own capture ran fast; delivery over venue Wi-Fi is bursty; time.time() steps on NTP/sleep-wake corrections (gig laptops), loop.time() does not. Probe (probe_jitter.py): bunched receipt stamps still detect (slope under-read 9 vs 15 dB/s) - the detector is fairly robust; the fragile part is the ts<=last drop and the mixed time bases.

**On a real desk:** A backward wall-clock step of N s during a session drops every frame for N s with no log line (detector blind, ring_out keeps raising - compounding finding 3); bursty delivery turns per-burst slopes into >60 dB/s 'onsets' that restart growth windows; '6 frames' of override persistence is 300 ms only at the nominal rate.

**Offline test:** FixtureSource replay of a recorded 15 dB/s ring with (a) receipt stamps bunched 4-per-200 ms, (b) a -2 s step in ts mid-stream: assert detection latency within 2x nominal and that cfs logs/aborts rather than silently discarding 40 frames. Fix: stamp LiveMeters frames with loop.time() (monotonic) or nominal index*period smoothed against receipt time; express persistence/override/verify in seconds.

> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (low)** — Citations check out and the core mechanism is real, but only one of the three claimed failure modes is substantiated.

CONFIRMED part: LiveMeters stamps every frame with wall-clock time at receipt (meters.py:392 `clock: Callable[[], float] = time.time`, :457 `ts = self._clock()`), all production constructions use that default (cfs.py:508, server.py:1432, server.py:1512), DESIGN.md:88 even specifies `ts: float # time.time()`, and CfsEngine._consume drops any frame whose ts is not strictly increasing with a bare `continue` — no log, no counter (cfs.py:1028-1029). The RAISE loop (cfs.py:1153-1198) never checks frame freshness (ses.frames / frame_event) before the next _write_master, so during a backward wall-clock step the detector is blind while the master keeps rising. My probe: a −2 s step in ts mid-stream drops exactly 40 frames (2.0 s) silently. meters.md §1.2 (line 73) and §6 item 7 (line 473) do say the 50 ms rate is nominal/'may be variable'; the tests/fixtures do hard-code ts=i*0.05 (test_detector.py:25,144) and SyntheticRta uses a perfect virtual clock (meters.py:582-583, :725); device.yaml:800 comment '2 s at 20 fps' is accurate. No fallback exists (clock is injectable but never injected with a monotonic source). Note meters.md §6.7 actually says 'timestamp locally', which the code does — the research does not demand a monotonic clock; that part of the argument rests on engineering common sense (NTP/timed steps), which the brief allows.

NOT substantiated: (a) 'bursty delivery turns per-burst slopes into >60 dB/s onsets that restart growth windows' — _ls_slope (detector.py:250-261) guards sxx<=0 and once one inter-burst gap is in the window the LS slope is moderate; my probe with 4-frames-per-200 ms bunching (300 µs apart) shows exactly one onset reset (first burst only) and detection at frame 5 instead of 2 with slope under-read 7.5 vs 15 dB/s — the claimant's own probe_jitter result says the same ('detector is fairly robust'). (b) 'Mixed time bases' — cooldown (detector.py:304-310/431) uses frame ts on both sides, VERIFY deadline (cfs.py:1229/1233) uses loop.time() on both sides, dwell (cfs.py:1131) is a relative timeout, reports (cfs.py:493/979) are display-only; no cross-clock comparison exists, so no concrete failure follows from the mixing itself. (c) '6 frames = 300 ms only at nominal rate' is true but cosmetic.

Real-gig likelihood of the confirmed part is low: it needs a backward step of the system clock (NTP/timed correction after joining venue Wi-Fi) during an active ring-out; sleep/wake steps forward, not backward. Severity low as the claimant rated: a latent silent-blindness path compounding the separately-reported 'RAISE ungated on frames' issue, cheap to fix (stamp with loop.time()/time.monotonic, log+count dropped frames).

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — What holds: LiveMeters stamps frames with time.time() at receipt (src/x32mcp/meters.py:392 default clock, :457 `ts = self._clock()`; constructed without a clock override at cfs.py:508 and server.py:1432/1512), and CfsEngine._consume silently `continue`s on any frame with ts <= last_ts (cfs.py:1028-1029, no log line, ses.frames not advanced). So a backward wall-clock step of N s does blind the detector for N s with nothing in the log. That is a real, cheap-to-fix hardening gap (stamp with time.monotonic()/loop.time(), log the drop) that no test can exercise because every fixture clock (test_detector.py i*0.05, SyntheticRta t0+i*period, zero-jitter loopback) is monotonic.

What does not hold / is already mitigated:
1. '20 fps assumed' is not an emulator-vs-desk mismatch: HANDOVER §4a records the real X32 streaming /meters/15 and /meters/1 'at 20 fps' on the wired LAN, exactly what FakeDesk/SyntheticRta reproduce. meters.md §6 pitfall 7 says 'Don't derive timing from packet arrival; timestamp locally' — which is what LiveMeters does.
2. The detector does not count on 50 ms frames for anything that matters: growth is a least-squares slope over the actual (ts, level) pairs (detector.py:333 _ls_slope(c.ts_list, c.levels)), cooldown is in seconds (detector.py:304-310, :431), VERIFY is a seconds deadline on loop.time() waiting on frame events (cfs.py:1228-1247), floor calibration is capped by floor_sample_s=2.0 with the 40-frame count only a 'whichever first' shortcut (device.yaml:799-800, cfs.py:857-861). The remaining frame-count constants (persistence 3, decay_verify 2, override 6) are small debounce counts where a ±50% period change is immaterial.
3. 'Mixed time bases' produce no actual cross-clock comparison: frame.ts is only compared with frame.ts (drop check, LS slope, cooldown); VERIFY/dwell/candidate-throttle use loop.time only against loop.time; time.time() in stages/reports is cosmetic (README 'Clocks' already tells the operator to keep the PC clock sane for ids). grep confirms frame.ts is consumed only at cfs.py:1028-1034 and webui.py:446.
4. Bursty delivery: the documented host is a Windows PC on the desk's wired LAN (README Requirements); Wi-Fi is the dashboard tablet. Even so, my own probe (scratchpad/probe_clock.py) feeding the real FeedbackDetector with receipt stamps bunched 4-per-200 ms and 10-per-500 ms shows first-detection latency within 0-3 frames of nominal for 6/8/10/15/20/30 dB/s rings: within-burst slopes (1500-5000 dB/s) trip the onset guard and cross-burst slopes under-read (~9-10 vs 15-20 dB/s), but the established-feedback override (25 dB prominence, 6 frames, detector.py:352-368) or the residual growth score still emits at essentially the same level. The finder's own probe reached the same conclusion ('fairly robust').
5. The backward-step scenario is improbable at a gig: it needs an NTP step (W32Time steps only when offset > ~1 s; macOS timed steps only large offsets, typically at wake) to land inside an attended 1-2 minute ring-out, on a PC that is usually on the desk's isolated subnet with no NTP reachable at all. Sleep/wake steps time forward, not backward, and kills the /xremote session anyway. If it did happen the blindness is bounded to N s (~1-2 extra 1 dB raises at step_db 1.0/dwell 1500 ms, device.yaml:826-827); the unbounded-raise risk belongs to the separate 'no frame-stall watchdog in ring_out' finding it says it compounds, not to this one.

Net: a valid low-severity robustness note (use a monotonic clock for frame ts; don't drop frames silently), not a wrong belief about the desk that the emulator certified, and not something that would plausibly bite with a real X32 on the documented wired setup. Severity low, as the finder already rated it.

## E62. [low] (cfs-detector-fixtures, confirmed) A notch is forever: once a -3 dB cut passes VERIFY the same band never rings again however much further the master is raised, so a ring-out is 'inject one ring, cut once, raise 11 dB more, DONE'.

**Encoded at:** tests/integration/test_cfs.py:319-356 (test_ring_out_closed_loop asserts names.count('NOTCH') == 1, 14 RAISEs, DONE at target -6 after feedback at ~-17), src/x32mcp/meters.py:714-718 (a cut larger than growth*period sends the ring to -128 and keeps it there regardless of later gain), fakedesk.py:44 (fader not coupled).

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/cfs.py:1164-1170,1216-1217 (after VERIFY ok the loop resumes stepping immediately; correctness of the multi-ring path - re-detect same band after cooldown, deepen, budget accounting, 'target reached' DONE - is only exercised open-loop in test_ring_out_untamable_ring_backs_off), report fields gain_before_feedback/max_master (cfs.py:1381-1384).

**Reality:** A -3 dB notch buys at most ~3 dB of headroom at that frequency (less off-centre, finding 13); the next steps re-ring the same band (deepen to -6/-9 = at most 9 dB total) or the next room mode - exactly Jim's account in HANDOVER §4b ('pushed the master higher, the next band up rang'). A DONE at 'target reached' 11 dB above first feedback with one -3 dB notch is not physically reachable.

**On a real desk:** No wrong write by itself (the state machine does handle re-rings), but the only closed-loop integration test certifies an impossible trajectory, so regressions in the deepen/re-verify/budget path against a live loop (e.g. stale pending re-detections dropped at cfs.py:1214-1215, cooldown vs VERIFY timing) cannot be caught, and README/report expectations ('target reached') are calibrated on it.

**Offline test:** With the LoopCoupledRing fixture (finding 5/9) plus a second mode (onset 3 dB higher at another frequency), assert the realistic trajectory: same band re-detected and deepened at +3 dB, second band opened, DONE/ABORT when 9 dB per band or the budget is exhausted, end_master <= first_onset + total cut - margin. The tau=5 ms run already shows it offline: notches at -16/-13/-10/-7 dB master, ABORT at -9 dB depth.

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (low)** — Both citations check out and no fallback was missed. (1) The fake really does encode "a notch is forever, independent of further gain": SyntheticRta._advance (src/x32mcp/meters.py:714-718) applies `level += growth*period_s - cut*period_s/loop_period_s` with loop_period_s defaulting to period_s, so a 3 dB cut against a 20 dB/s ring (1 dB/frame) nets -2 dB/frame to the -128 floor and holds it there; the ring's growth term has no fader/master input, and FakeDesk._refresh_cuts (fakedesk.py:1103-1135) derives RTA cuts from the GEQ pars only. fakedesk.py:44 states this outright: "The bus fader/mute is deliberately *not* coupled to ring growth." The docstring at meters.py:572-578 even advertises "one -3 dB GEQ step kills any ring slower than 60 dB/s". (2) The only closed-loop ring_out integration test certifies the resulting impossible trajectory: tests/integration/test_cfs.py:319-356 injects one ring at master >= -18, then asserts final_stage DONE, max_master -6, end -9, budget_left 5, len(notches)==1 at -3 dB, names.count('RAISE')==14 and names.count('NOTCH')==1 — i.e. ~11-12 dB of extra gain bought by a single -3 dB cut. (3) Reality per HANDOVER §4b (docs/HANDOVER.md:145-147): "the ring started, a notch killed it; he pushed the master higher, the next band up rang, and that was caught too. Then the notch budget (4) ran out" — the real trajectory is notch -> a few dB -> next ring -> ... -> budget spent, consistent with unity-loop-gain physics (a -3 dB cut at the ring frequency restores at most ~3 dB of margin there). (4) Code-dependence claim is accurately scoped by the claimant: cfs.py:1164-1170 (after a tamed ring the loop `continue`s and resumes RAISE toward target), 1214-1217 (stale pending re-detections of the band dropped, return True on ok) are correct cites; the "VERIFY ok -> raise -> same/next band re-detected -> HOLD again" path and the `reason = "notch budget spent"` DONE exits (cfs.py:1164-1166, 1171-1173) are asserted by no test anywhere (grep of tests/ for "budget spent" finds only the NotchController unit test at test_detector.py:440); test_ring_out_untamable_ring_backs_off (test_cfs.py:403-429) covers only deepen-in-place to -9 -> ABORT with an open-loop RTA, and test_feedback_watch_closed_loop is single ring/single notch. Deepen/budget/cooldown logic is unit-tested in test_detector.py (393, 431, 246-249), so this is partly "coverage of already-tested logic", and the decoupling is a documented, deliberate simplification rather than an unwitting belief — hence low, as the claimant rated it: no wrong write, no safety impact, the state machine does handle re-rings. Minor overstatement: README.md:713-724 describes both exits (target or budget spent) and is not "calibrated" on the one-notch trajectory. The proposed offline test (fader-coupled ring via the claimant's LoopCoupledRing helper in $SP/reports/assumptions-cfs-detector-fixtures/test_assumptions_cfs.py:134-163 plus a second mode, asserting re-detection/deepen, a second notch, and DONE 'notch budget spent' or ABORT at -9 dB with end_master bounded by onset + total cut - margin) is the right shape and would fail against today's test expectations.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The factual core holds: the stock closed-loop fixture decouples ring growth from the bus master (fakedesk.py:42-44 says so explicitly: "The bus fader/mute is deliberately *not* coupled to ring growth") and SyntheticRta._advance (meters.py:714-718) makes any cut larger than growth*loop_period drive the ring to -128 and hold it there regardless of later fader moves, so test_ring_out_closed_loop (tests/integration/test_cfs.py:319-356) does certify a physically unreachable trajectory — one -3 dB notch at ~-17 dB, then 11 more 1 dB raises with names.count('NOTCH') == 1, DONE 'target reached' at -6, back-off to -9. A real loop re-rings the same band ~3 dB later (or the next mode), exactly as HANDOVER §4b records.

But arguing from the gig consequence, nothing bites: (1) no product code depends on the notch being permanent — _run_ringout (cfs.py:1146-1196) pops re-detections into HOLD, _notch/NotchController deepens -3/-6/-9 and ABORTs 'not tamed' with a forced 6 dB back-off; (2) that path is covered piecewise offline — NotchController -3/-6/-9/None and budget exhaustion (tests/test_detector.py:393-442), detector re-emission once per cooldown for a band that keeps ringing (test_detector.py:246-249), deepen+VERIFY-fail loop end-to-end through the Desk (test_ring_out_untamable_ring_backs_off, test_cfs.py:403-430); (3) it was demonstrated on the real X32 (HANDOVER §4b: notch killed the ring, master pushed, next band rang, caught, budget ran out — the state machine did the right thing); (4) I ran the originating slice's own LoopCoupledRing probe (worktree assumptions-cfs-detector-fixtures, tests/integration/test_assumptions_cfs.py:134-186, tau=5 ms) and the closed-loop re-ring-same-band path behaves physically today: 'master -20.0 -> -13.0 dB (highest -7.0), 1 notch, feedback first at -16.0 dB; ABORT: ring at 2500 Hz not tamed' — i.e. detect at -16, re-detect and deepen at -13/-10, refuse at -7, back off 6 dB. That probe's failure is about catch latency/level (a different finding), not about the re-ring/deepen/budget logic. README §ring_out (README.md:713-724) describes deepen/abort correctly and does not promise 'target reached'.

So what remains is a test-realism/coverage observation: the only stock closed-loop integration test enshrines an impossible single-notch +11 dB run and the 'VERIFY ok → raise → same band re-rings → new HOLD → deepen' sequence has no regression test in the main suite. No wrong write, no tool reporting wrong state, no spurious failure at a gig; it sits close to the brief's 'missing tests for already-tested logic' exclusion. Worth fixing by promoting a loop-coupled fixture into tests/integration and asserting the realistic trajectory, but severity stays low as the finder already conceded.

## E63. [low] (desk-policy-server, confirmed) A full ~2100-node pre-write snapshot is cheap enough to sit in front of the session's first Tier-1 write (the fake answers 2103 /node requests in ~0.3 s with zero loss and zero latency).

**Encoded at:** tests/integration/conftest.py (loopback, fakedesk.latency_ms=0, no drops); test_desk.py:410-422 and test_server_tools.py:191 assert the snapshot is taken, never how long the first write takes on a real link; HANDOVER §4a measured 0.28 s on wired LAN only.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/desk.py:871-877 _write -> ensure_pre_write_snapshot (desk.py:846-862, dump of every node) before conn.set; applies to mute/set_fader/adjust_*/set_eq_band/label; only panic() skips it (desk.py:1186). DESIGN §0.5: 'worst case for any tool is ~2 s'.

**Reality:** transport.md §2/§10 (DOC 269-274, 2900-2907): bulk /node bursts over 54 Mb/s Wi-Fi lose datagrams silently; each loss costs a 0.5 s retry; RTT at FOH over venue Wi-Fi is tens of ms (device.yaml:731-734 itself describes the operator on a phone at FOH). Measured offline: fakedesk.latency_ms=25 -> first set_mute takes 3.6 s (red test test_first_mute_of_the_session_is_fast_on_a_slow_link).

**On a real desk:** 'The vocal mic is howling, mute ch 4' as the first write of the session: the mute reaches the desk 3-10 s later (sweep + retries) while the room listens to the howl; an LLM told about one channel calls mute/adjust_fader, not panic. Under loss the snapshot also lands with `missing` sections that the write tool never mentions, so the promised undo has silent holes.

**Offline test:** Set fakedesk.latency_ms=25 (and drop_next some replies) and assert the first desk.set_mute completes < 2 s and that the tool envelope surfaces snapshot `missing`; today 3.6 s and silent. Direction: take the snapshot at connect()/idle time or in the background, or snapshot only the section being written first and complete the sweep after the write.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — Mechanism CONFIRMED, consequence overstated, severity downgraded to low.

What is true: Desk._write (src/x32mcp/desk.py:871-877) awaits ensure_pre_write_snapshot (desk.py:846-862) → Desk.dump → nodes.dump_desk_state over all 2103 descriptor nodes (nodes.py:716-750, conn.node_many concurrency 16, connection.py:556-572) before conn.set for every Tier-1 write path (mute/set_fader/adjust_*/set_eq_band/label, plus server.py:1399 and 1477); only panic() bypasses. The integration fixtures run the fake at latency_ms=0 with no loss (tests/integration/conftest.py) and the only tests touching this (tests/integration/test_desk.py:416-424, test_server_tools.py:191) assert THAT the snapshot was taken, never what the first write costs. Reproduced in my own worktree with production timeouts (0.5 s × 3): first set_mute = 0.08 s @RTT 0, 0.39 s @2 ms, 0.88 s @5 ms, 1.6 s @10 ms, 3.6 s @25 ms, 4.5 s @5 ms+5 % loss (1 section silently missing from the undo snapshot), 4.8 s @25 ms+2 % loss; second write always ~0 ms. So DESIGN §0 principle 5 ('worst case for any tool is ~2 s') is violated on a slow/lossy link, and the finder's red test (3.6 s) is accurate for the RTT it chose.

Why it would rarely bite at a gig: (1) The documented and live-tested topology is a PC on the desk's LAN (README:289, GIG_CHECKLIST 'Desk, PC and tablet on the same LAN'); on that link the real desk answered the full sweep in 0.28 s (HANDOVER §4a) and the zero-latency fake reproduces that almost exactly — for the primary deployment the fake is faithful, not optimistic. (2) 25 ms is not 'a good venue Wi-Fi round trip' — local Wi-Fi RTT is typically 2-8 ms, giving 0.4-1.5 s by measurement; '3-10 s' needs a congested 2.4 GHz link with percent-level UDP loss. (4) The emergency path does not pay it: panic() skips it (desk.py:1186), CFS² deliberately hoists the snapshot into _arm so notches are not delayed (cfs.py:901-909 — the authors knew the dump is slow), and GIG_CHECKLIST:10 states the plan for mid-set trouble is the physical mute/X32-Edit with panic() as backstop; a voice→LLM→tool round trip already costs several seconds, so +0.4-2 s on one write is a degradation, not a new failure class. (5) It is a conscious BRIEF §4 requirement ('before the first Tier 1/2 write in a session, dump full desk state'), and the design openly budgets seconds for a dump (DESIGN §20 'dump < 5 s', snapshot_desk docstring 'Takes a few seconds on a real desk', DUMP_TIMEOUT_S=60) — a known trade-off (undo net vs first-write latency), not a hidden belief the emulator certified. No wrong write, no safety action on garbage, no tool reporting wrong state → does not meet the brief's 'medium' bar.

Residual, real but minor: (a) the 'missing' sections of a lossy auto-snapshot are only logged/evented (desk.py:855, 860), never surfaced in the write tool's envelope, so the promised undo can have unannounced holes (1 section at 5 % loss in my run); (b) a manual snapshot_desk (server.py:1180-1192 — the GIG_CHECKLIST pre-show step) does not call mark_snapshot_taken, so the checklist does not move the cost out of the show and the desk is swept twice; (c) if a tool timeout ever cancels the dump (ramped set_fader budget = ramp+15 s, server.py:430-446; mute 30 s) the flag stays armed and every later Tier-1 write re-pays the sweep — a livelock, but only on a link needing >15 s per sweep, i.e. one on which nothing works anyway. Cheap fixes: take the auto snapshot at connect()/idle in the background, let snapshot_desk disarm it, and echo snapshot.missing in the first write's envelope.

Second probe confirms the Desk knew: '/ch/01/mix' is absent from desk._cache after the dump (dropped because pushed) yet state.get('/ch/01/mix/fader') == 0.0. So the fix is cheap (copy _dropped_since into state.torn and re-read those sections, or refuse/label the snapshot) and the FakeDesk is already capable of the real behaviour — the assumption lives in the idle-desk tests and in dump() discarding the information, not in the emulator.

Why it stays low, argued from the gig: (1) the window is one sweep — 0.28 s on the wired link the deployment prescribes (HANDOVER §4a; README:289 puts the PC on the LAN and Wi-Fi only on the dashboard tablet); 'seconds on Wi-Fi' is a sibling finding's extrapolation from transport.md §2/§10 datagram-loss warnings, not a real-desk observation. (2) The auto pre-write sweep is triggered by Claude's first write, asynchronous to the engineer, so a scene recall/channel paste has to land inside that 0.3 s by coincidence; a lone fader ride captured mid-travel is not a chimera (each section is one atomic /node reply). (3) restore never writes 'verbatim': restore_plan (nodes.py:1201-1227) writes only sections differing from a fresh live dump, and restore_snapshot is Tier 2 — the first call previews 'N setting(s) in M section(s) would change' with the first 15 English diffs and requires a confirm token (server.py:1240-1262), so a half-old-band restore is visible to the operator before it is written. (4) diff_snapshot does not attribute changes, so 'phantom changes' is overstated — it reports true file-vs-desk differences, merely against a misleading baseline. (5) No OSC client can snapshot 2100 sections atomically (Maillot's X32GetScene has the same property), and transport.md §4.1 notes some desk actions are not pushed at all, so even push-based torn detection is best-effort. Net: a genuine, cheaply fixable gap in the same class as the brief's examples, correctly rated low.

The worst plausible outcome is a cautious model re-requesting confirmation once between 60 and 300 s -- an extra prompt for the operator, no wrong write, no safety impact. ## E68. [low] (fakedesk-fidelity, partial) A GEQ cut on the ISO band nearest the detected RTA band lands with its full depth on the ringing frequency, and any cut larger than the ring's per-frame growth (0.75 dB) kills the ring regardless of how far above unity the loop is.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1129-1134 (_refresh_cuts maps every RTA band to the log-nearest GEQ centre and applies that band's FULL gain — a rectangular 1/3-octave brick wall) which is the same function as src/x32mcp/detector.py:539-543 NotchController.band_for_freq, so detector and fake can never disagree (a closed loop like parser-vs-renderer); src/x32mcp/meters.py:572-578,714-718 'level -= cut per frame' (one -3 dB step kills any ring slower than 60 dB/s by construction). Relied on by tests/integration/test_cfs.py:281-284, 340-345 (one -3 dB notch, VERIFY passes first time), test_fakedesk.py:420-427.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/detector.py:551-575 (plan: one nearest band, notch_step -3, merge_adjacent_bands 1 only for re-detections); src/x32mcp/cfs.py:1201-1219 (_notch_and_verify deepens the SAME band until -9 then declares 'not tamed' and aborts, cfs.py:1160-1163); det.freq_hz is the 1/10-octave RTA band centre, not the ring frequency.

**Reality:** fx_routing_scenes.md §2.3: GEQ bands are ISO 1/3-octave bells 20 Hz-20 kHz (31 centres); a graphic-EQ band set to -3 dB reaches -3 dB only at its centre and roughly half that (in dB) at the ±1/6-octave band edge, and the RTA quantises the ring to a 1/10-octave centre (meters.md §4.2 formula) — a ring at 2240 Hz (between 2k and 2.5k) reads as RTA band 68 (2176 Hz) → GEQ 2 kHz, whose -3 dB cut is ≈-1.5 dB at 2240 Hz. Physically a notch tames a ring only if the effective cut exceeds the loop-gain excess at that frequency (finding 3), not a fixed 0.75 dB/frame. HANDOVER §4b: real cuts measured -5.9/-6.0/-3.9 across three adjacent RTA bands for one GEQ band — a shaped response, not a brick wall.

**On a real desk:** Rings that sit between ISO centres (half of them, statistically) are systematically under-cut: VERIFY fails, the same band is driven to -9 dB (a 9 dB hole a third-octave away from the problem), the neighbour band that would have helped is never touched (merge_adjacent_bands only deepens existing notches), and ring_out aborts with 'not tamed' while the wedge still rings. In feedback_watch after a +5 dB shove the -3 dB step is simply insufficient and the fake cannot express that.

**Offline test:** Give SyntheticRta/FakeDesk a bell response per GEQ band evaluated at each RTA band centre (e.g. RBJ peaking magnitude with the X32 GEQ's Q≈4.3, or linear-in-dB interpolation between centres for TEQ) and sum overlapping bands; keep the true ring frequency (not the band centre) for the loop-gain computation. Add rings at 2240, 1120, 4470 Hz (geometric means of ISO pairs) to test_ring_out_closed_loop and assert DONE with ≤-6 dB total and no -9 single-band hole; today the brick-wall fake passes trivially and the shaped fake would abort.

That is a design limitation an engineer standing at the desk resolves by pulling the fader; in ring_out (excess ≤ step_db) it costs at most one extra 1.5 s VERIFY and a 3 dB deeper hole 1/6 oct off. Not a wrong write, not a false report, already bounded by the deepen loop + back-off → downgrade to low.

## E69. [low] (fakedesk-fidelity, partial) /save (scene store) is answered instantly, so the generic request/retry path (0.5 s per attempt, 2 re-sends) is appropriate for it.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1159-1184 (_h_save copies state and replies ',si scene 1' synchronously in the same datagram handler; _save_scene_file is a local JSON write); tests/integration/test_desk.py:466, test_server_tools.py:286 (save dance) and test_fakedesk.py:454 pass with the 0.25 s test timeout.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/desk.py:1290-1310 save_scene → conn.request('/save', …) with default timeout_s 0.5 × (retries 2 + 1) (connection.py:245-246, 747-769: every retry RE-SENDS the datagram); a RequestTimeout becomes DeskError TIMEOUT / SCENE_FAILED although nothing says the save failed.

**Reality:** fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4 gives only the reply form (/save ,si scene 1); transport.md §5.4: real-desk latency UNCONFIRMED, Maillot's tools poll with 10-100 ms for parameter reads but a scene store writes ~2000 parameters to flash and the front panel visibly takes a moment; HANDOVER §4a: scene save/recall were NOT verified at M5 (desk was in CUES). /save is not idempotent in effect-free terms: each datagram is another flash write with whatever state exists at that instant. Probe test_probe_slow_save_is_not_duplicated_or_misreported (600 ms reply latency) fails today: '/save reached the desk 2 times' and save_scene raised.

**On a real desk:** save_scene('pre-show') before doors: the desk takes ~0.6-1 s, the server re-sends /save twice more (three stores, the later ones possibly capturing a fader mid-move), then reports TIMEOUT/SCENE_FAILED; the model tells the engineer the safety scene was NOT saved and may retry or pick another slot, littering the show file — or worse, the engineer distrusts a scene that is actually fine.

**Offline test:** FakeDesk switch save_latency_ms (reply after N ms, default 0) and a counter of /save datagrams; test: with save_latency 800 ms save_scene must send exactly one /save (retries=0 for non-idempotent commands, timeout ≥3 s) and return ok, and must verify by reading /-show/showfile/scene/NNN hasdata/name afterwards instead of trusting/doubting the single reply.

> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (low)** — Code citations check out: FakeDesk._h_save (src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1159-1184) replies '/save ,si scene 1' in the same handler call; Desk.save_scene (src/x32mcp/desk.py:1290-1310) calls conn.request('/save', ...) with no timeout/retries override, so production defaults timeout_s=0.5, retries=2 apply (connection.py:245-246; App builds X32Connection with conn_opts=None, server.py:154), and _request_bytes (connection.py:747-769) re-sends the datagram on every attempt; a RequestTimeout becomes DeskError TIMEOUT with no post-hoc check of /-show/showfile/scene/NNN/hasdata|name. HANDOVER §4a (lines 130-132) confirms scene save/recall were never exercised on the real desk (show control was CUES), and transport.md §5.4 (line 358) marks real-desk reply latency UNCONFIRMED. So the assumption class is real: the fake answers /save in 0 ms and nothing verifies the real timing.

But the claimant's 'reality' and failure narrative are miscalibrated and partly unsupported: (1) fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4 does not 'give only the reply form' — line 564 quotes DOC fn.39-41 'The load/save/copy operation is not necessarily fully completed when the status is returned', i.e. the documented behaviour is that the desk returns the status BEFORE the store finishes, which undercuts the claim that the flash write delays the reply; the '~2000 parameters to flash / front panel takes a moment' premise appears in no research or handover text. (2) §5.4 recommends 50-100 ms with one retry; the code's 0.5 s x 3 is already 5-15x more lenient than the research, not tighter. (3) My probe under PRODUCTION defaults (only the /save reply delayed) shows: 0.6-0.9 s -> ok with 2 datagrams (the late first reply satisfies attempt 2's waiter), 1.2 s -> ok with 3, and a false TIMEOUT only when the reply takes >1.5 s. The claimant's 'save_scene raised at 600 ms' came from the test harness's shortened 0.25 s x 2 connection, and 'three stores then TIMEOUT at 0.6-1 s' is wrong for production. (4) A duplicate /save to the same slot with the same name/notes <=0.5 s apart is benign in effect (the slot ends up holding essentially the same state); it is not a wrong write in the safety sense. Real residual issues: a false TIMEOUT if a real desk ever exceeds 1.5 s (speculative, contradicted in tendency by fn.39-41), no verify-after-timeout fallback, and the late '/save' reply being cached as a parameter and published as an 'update' event (connection.py:832-834). Net: valid but speculative assumption, overstated consequence -> PARTIAL, low.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The assumption is real and encoded exactly where the finding says: FakeDesk._h_save (src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1159-1184) stores and replies `,si scene 1` synchronously, and Desk.save_scene (src/x32mcp/desk.py:1290-1310) pushes the non-idempotent `/save` through the generic X32Connection.request path (connection.py:243-246 defaults timeout_s=0.5, retries=2; _request_bytes 747-769 re-sends the datagram on every retry) with no read-back of /-show/showfile/scene/NNN afterwards. Real-desk /save latency is UNCONFIRMED (transport.md §5.4) and HANDOVER §4a confirms save_scene was never exercised live (desk in CUES), so the code does depend on an unverified number without a fallback. I reproduced it offline with the FakeDesk's existing `latency_ms` switch under production connection defaults: 0/400 ms -> 1 datagram, ok; 600 ms -> 2 /save datagrams reach the desk but save_scene returns ok (attempt 2's waiter is satisfied by attempt 1's late reply, matched by address; the second reply is then cached as an unsolicited '/save' param); 1200 ms -> 3 datagrams, ok; 1600 ms -> 3 datagrams and DeskError TIMEOUT although the scene was stored. Maillot's real-desk tools (X32GetLib.c:801-830, X32SetLib.c:783-808) corroborate the design point: they send /save exactly once and block in an unbounded `while (Xlock) RPOLL` loop commented 'Wait for save to complete' — never re-sending.

However, as a skeptical verifier I downgrade it. (1) The one piece of VERIFIED ground truth on timing points the other way: fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4 quotes DOC fn.39-41, 'The load/save/copy operation is not necessarily fully completed when the status is returned' — i.e. the desk returns the status before the flash write finishes, so the '~0.6-1 s reply' premise is speculation, and the >1.5 s needed for the false TIMEOUT/SCENE_FAILED is unlikely on a wired LAN. (2) The finding's own probe claim is overstated: at 600 ms save_scene does NOT raise; it returns ok with a duplicate store. (3) The duplicate stores go to the same slot with the same name/notes within 0.5 s of each other, so the show file is not 'littered' and the audible/operational consequence is nil; 'fader mid-move during a pre-show safety save' is contrived. (4) The misreport, if it ever happened, is recoverable by list_scenes and writes nothing wrong to audio paths. Net: a legitimate robustness gap (non-idempotent command on a re-sending retry path, unverified latency, no verification read-back) worth fixing as proposed (retries=0, timeout of a few seconds, confirm via scene/NNN hasdata/name), but the realistic gig impact is cosmetic-to-none, not 'tool reports wrong state at a gig'.

## E70. [low] (fakedesk-fidelity, partial) RTA frames arrive exactly every 50 ms with strictly increasing, high-resolution timestamps, so a least-squares slope over arrival times is the ring's true dB/s and equal timestamps mean a duplicate frame.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:913-922 (_meter_stream: asyncio.sleep(interval) pacing, no jitter, no bursts, no drops; latency_ms is a constant offset, :778-781); src/x32mcp/meters.py:723-728,753-760 SyntheticRta stamps frames on a virtual clock t0+i·period (perfect spacing) and tests/test_detector.py feeds those; all integration tests run on macOS/Linux µs clocks.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/meters.py:390,454-466 LiveMeters stamps frames with time.time() at datagram arrival; src/x32mcp/detector.py:326-343 growth = LS slope over (arrival ts, level), onset guard resets when slope > 60 dB/s; src/x32mcp/cfs.py:1028-1029 drops any frame whose ts <= last ts as 'duplicate/reordered'.

**Reality:** meters.md §1.2/§6 gotcha 7: 'Update cycle … may be variable according to console's ability to fulfill requests … Don't derive timing from packet arrival'; the DOC's own tf=80 capture ran ~25% fast. Over Wi-Fi (HANDOVER §2/§3: Termux/phone is a stated target; DOC warns about Wi-Fi) power-save and retransmission deliver UDP in clumps (3-4 frames within 1 ms after a 150-200 ms gap). On the Windows desk PC (HANDOVER §2: CPython 3.12) time.time() ticks at 15.625 ms (GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime only from 3.13), so frames in one recv batch get IDENTICAL timestamps.

**On a real desk:** A steady 20 dB/s ring delivered as a clump computes as hundreds of dB/s → onset guard resets it (missed/late notch); a plateaued music note whose frames clump looks like growth → false notch; on Windows every clumped frame after the first is silently discarded by cfs as a duplicate, halving the effective frame rate exactly when the network is struggling, and persistence/override frame counts stretch accordingly.

**Offline test:** FakeDesk switch frame_jitter: deliver meter datagrams in bursts (hold k frames, release together) and with ±20 ms jitter; LiveMeters option to stamp frames as first_ts + n·(0.05·tf) (sequence-derived) or to pass a coarse clock (lambda: round(time.time()/0.015625)*0.015625) in tests. Assert test_feedback_watch_closed_loop still notches within 1 s with bursts of 4 and that no frames are dropped with the 15.6 ms clock; today the coarse-clock variant drops 3 of every 4 clumped frames.

> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (low)** — Code citations check out: fakedesk.py:913-922 paces meter datagrams with a bare asyncio.sleep(interval) (no jitter/burst/drop knob; latency_ms at :778-779 is a constant offset); meters.py:725 SyntheticRta stamps t0+i*period; tests/test_detector.py:3/25 declare 'frame i is at t = i*0.05 s'; LiveMeters stamps at datagram receipt with clock=time.time (meters.py:391 default, :454-457), and cfs.py:508 / server.py:1432,1512 construct LiveMeters without overriding clock; detector.py:334-339 computes an LS slope over (arrival ts, level) and resets the growth window when slope > 60 dB/s; cfs.py:1028-1029 silently drops any frame with ts <= last_ts. HANDOVER §2 confirms the gig host is Windows 10 + CPython 3.12.14, where time.time() (GetSystemTimeAsFileTime) and time.monotonic() tick at 15.625 ms (precise clocks only from 3.13) — so on the real host, any two datagrams processed within one tick get identical stamps and the second is discarded. Nothing in the suite exercises irregular arrival, so the assumption is genuinely encoded and untested.

However: (1) The research citation is misapplied. meters.md §6 gotcha 7 reads 'Frame rate is nominal … Don't derive timing from packet arrival; timestamp locally' — i.e. do not assume N frames = N×50 ms, stamp with the local clock on receipt, which is exactly what LiveMeters does; the claimant's proposed fix (sequence-derived first_ts + n·0.05·tf) is what the research warns against. §1.2's tf=80 note likewise argues for arrival stamping, not against it. HANDOVER has no Wi-Fi observation; Wi-Fi clumping is plausible only for the Termux target (fine clock), and on the wired Windows PC clumping needs an event-loop stall ≥50 ms or desk-side bunching — hypothesised, not observed (dispatch is synchronous in datagram_received, connection.py:203/826, so consumer-side awaits in cfs do not clump stamps). (2) The claimed consequences are overstated. I ran the test suite's own SyntheticRta ring (2.5 kHz, start -60 dB) through FeedbackDetector with the shipped device.yaml config under different stamp models: perfect 50 ms → first detection frame 131 (20 dB/s), slope 18.4, conf 0.96; bursts of 4 with a µs clock → frame 134, slope 9.9, conf 0.75 (late by 150 ms, not missed; at 10 dB/s late by 450 ms, conf 0.72); 15.6 ms clock alone → identical to perfect; 15.6 ms clock + bursts of 4 → 300/400 frames dropped (confirmed) but detection at frame 140 with correct slope 20.3 (≈450 ms / +9 dB later). The 'plateaued note clumps into a false notch' did not occur — clumping removed the two marginal melody detections rather than adding any (constant y gives ~0 LS slope regardless of x spacing; tiny-window noise slopes exceed 60 dB/s and are zeroed by the onset guard). (3) A fallback the claimant missed: the established-feedback override (detector.py:350-372, override_prominence_db=25, 6 frames) emits regardless of growth, so timing corruption can delay/louden a notch but cannot make a real howl go un-notched.

Net: real, untested assumption with a concrete Windows-3.12 duplicate-drop interaction, but the research does not say what is claimed, the trigger on the actual host is speculative, measured impact is a few hundred ms of extra ring rather than missed/false notches, and the override bounds it. PARTIAL, low.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The encoded assumption is real and correctly located: FakeDesk paces meter datagrams with a bare `await asyncio.sleep(sub.interval_s)` and a constant `latency_ms` offset (src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:913-923, 771-781) — no jitter, bursts or drops are expressible; SyntheticRta stamps frames on a perfect virtual clock `t0 + frame_index*period_s` (src/x32mcp/meters.py:723) and every detector/cfs test consumes those stamps; production stamps frames with `time.time()` at datagram arrival (meters.py:390 default clock, :454-456), the detector's growth term is an LS slope over those arrival stamps with an onset-guard reset above 60 dB/s (detector.py:250-261, 326-337), and cfs discards any frame with `ts <= last_ts` (cfs.py:1028-1029). meters.md §1.2/§6 gotcha 7 does say the 50 ms cadence is nominal/variable, and CPython<=3.12 on Windows (the desk PC per HANDOVER §2, allowed by pyproject requires-python>=3.11) really does have a 15.6 ms time.time() (GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime only from 3.13).

I reproduced the mechanisms offline by feeding SyntheticRta frames to FeedbackDetector under different timestamp regimes with the cfs duplicate-drop applied (scripts in $SP/reports/verify-timing/exp*.py): (a) coarse 15.625 ms clock + 4-frame clumps: exactly 3 of every 4 frames are dropped as 'duplicates' (150/200), first detection of a 20 dB/s ring moves from frame 16.4 to 24 (+0.38 s, ring ~7.6 dB louder), 30 dB/s ring 12.2 -> 20; (b) microsecond clock + 4-frame clumps: ring detection only 1.6 frames late at 20 dB/s (18.0 vs 16.4) and 7.4 frames late at 10 dB/s (33.9 vs 26.5) — late, never missed, so the 'hundreds of dB/s -> missed notch' claim is overstated; but a NEW effect the finding only half-states is confirmed: a rock-steady held note of 16 dB prominence (below the 25 dB override) that yields 0 false detections in 16 000 ideally-timed frames yields 52-70 false detections when frames arrive in clumps of 3-4, because sub-0.04 dB level wiggles across a 0.6 ms clump compute as 8-60 dB/s 'growth' (confidence 1.0) — in WATCH mode each is a real -3 dB GEQ write. (c) The regimes that a wired desk LAN actually produces — +-10-20 ms jitter, the 15.6 ms Windows clock at nominal 50 ms spacing, and an occasional 2-frame clump from an event-loop stall — change nothing: identical detection frames, zero false positives, at most the second frame of a rare 2-clump silently dropped on Windows 3.12.

Why only PARTIAL/low: the trigger is sustained >=3-frame clumping, which is a property of a power-saving Wi-Fi receive path, not of the X32. The documented v1 deployment is a Windows PC on the desk LAN with only the dashboard (TCP) on a Wi-Fi tablet (BRIEF.md:9,89-91; README.md:289,784-793 — Termux/Wi-Fi host explicitly 'not built or tested in v1'), and HANDOVER §4a records /meters/15 and /meters/1 streaming at a clean 20 fps from the real desk. meters.md gotcha 7's actual advice ('timestamp locally') is what LiveMeters does; the finding's proposed sequence-derived stamping (first_ts + n*0.05*tf) contradicts the same gotcha and the DOC's tf=80 capture running ~25% fast. So at the planned gig with a real X32 this does not bite; it becomes a genuine medium/high (false GEQ cuts on sustained pads/organ in WATCH, ~0.4 s later notches, 5 fps effective on Windows<=3.12) the day the OSC path crosses power-saving Wi-Fi (Termux milestone or an ad-hoc laptop-on-venue-Wi-Fi), and the suite cannot express that today. Cheap hardening worth doing before M9: stamp with a high-resolution monotonic clock (time.perf_counter/monotonic — also immune to NTP steps that would make cfs drop frames as 'reordered'), and de-clump in the detector (ignore slope when the window's time span is < ~2 frame periods, or space clumped arrivals at a floor of period/2) plus a FakeDesk burst/jitter knob and a held-note-under-bursts test that fails today.

Tests cited exist and do certify via emulator state: tests/integration/test_desk.py:359-369 (panic asserts fakedesk.get(.../mix/on)==0 for all 24), tests/integration/test_cfs.py:270/359/427 (notch via fakedesk.get('/fx/5/par/22')), tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:134-139 (dump, missing==[]; path is tests/integration/, not tests/). Research citations are accurate: transport.md:149 §2 'Plain UDP, no ACK, no error report. DOC warns that burst /node or /showdump traffic over 54 Mb/s Wi-Fi loses datagrams silently'; :340 §5 'No ack. If you need confirmation, GET it back or hold /xremote on a second socket'; :536 §6.6 '/' echo 'use that echo as flow control'; :648 §10 Xdelay 1 ms / -t 10 ms; fx_routing_scenes.md:715 microsleep(100). HANDOVER.md:114 confirms '24/24 verified muted on the desk and confirmed visually' once (wired implied by the cable-pull test at :118; 'gigabit' is the claimant's embellishment, not in the doc).

What does not hold: (1) 'restore_plan later rewrites those sections from a holey snapshot' is wrong — nodes.py:1213-1215 `want = target_state.sections.get(node.path); if want is None: continue` skips sections missing from the snapshot (module doc :49 'sections missing from either state are skipped'); moreover /node reads retry 3x (connection.py:747-768) and misses are recorded in DeskState.missing and logged (desk.py:855-860), and restore writes use `slash()` which awaits the '/' echo with retries (connection.py:542-554), so the dump/restore leg is largely mitigated (the claimant half-concedes this: 'it does'). (2) 'bookkeeping wrong from then on' after a lost -3 notch is overstated: the deepen writes an absolute -6, after which writer.gains and the desk agree again; only the notch_log's -3 entry is fictitious and the cut ends 3 dB deeper than needed — divergence persists only if the lost SET was the last permitted (notch_max_db/budget). (3) The research partly cuts the other way: transport.md:649 'Overrun risk is on the receive side' and fx_routing_scenes.md:715 'the desk accepts many UDP messages back to back', and DESIGN.md:574 deliberately specifies panic as 'fire-and-forget sets' — so the desk-can't-absorb-a-24-datagram-burst angle is weak; the surviving risk is generic link loss (venue Wi-Fi), which the DOC itself warns about. Normal Tier-1/2 writes are also paced by the policy token bucket (policy.py:375-396), panic excepted.

Net: the assumption (a sent SET was applied; only replies get lost) is genuinely encoded in the fake and the tests, and panic, CFS notch writes and the DONE/ABORT back-off have no confirmation or fallback — a lost datagram makes panic report 'muted: 24' / a back-off report end_master_db that the bus never reached. That matches REVIEW_BRIEF §5's own ask for a '/'-echo/read-your-writes ack. Severity medium is fair for the panic/back-off mis-report conditional on loss (low probability on wired 100BASE-T, real on congested venue Wi-Fi); the snapshot/restore sub-claim is refuted. Offline test proposal (seedable inbound_loss_rate / rx burst capacity on FakeDesk; panic must GET-back and re-send or list unconfirmed keys; notch confirmed before VERIFY) is sound and would fail today.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — Core mechanism CONFIRMED, two sub-claims REFUTED, real-gig likelihood low -> PARTIAL, downgraded to low.

CONFIRMED part (fidelity gap is real): FakeDesk can only lose datagrams on the way BACK. fakedesk.py:792-799 `_reply` is the only place `_drop_left` is consulted; `_on_datagram` (fakedesk.py:750-769) decodes and applies every inbound datagram synchronously, and `silent` (761) is all-or-nothing. So no test in the suite can ever exercise 'a write that was sent but not applied', and tests/integration/test_desk.py:358-369 (24/24 mutes asserted by reading fakedesk state) is tautological with respect to delivery. Research disagrees with the fake: transport.md §2 'Plain UDP, no ACK, no error report ... loses datagrams silently'; §5.2 'No ack. If you need confirmation, GET it back'; §9 item 7 'silence = ignored or lost'. Code that depends on delivery without read-back: desk.py:1184-1222 panic() returns muted=[24 keys] and server.py:1070-1071 prints 'PANIC: 24 outputs muted ... (sent)' with no GET; desk.py:871-884 `_write` is fire-and-forget (cache invalidated, nothing re-sent); cfs.py:410-416 `_DeskGeqWriter.set_band_gain` records gains[band] after an unacknowledged `set_geq_band` (desk.py:1403-1431); cfs.py:1115-1124 `_write_master` takes `after_db` from `_move_level`, which is the intended value not a read-back (desk.py:955-974), so the DONE/ABORT BACKOFF level in the report is unconfirmed (only `_restore_master` on connection loss, cfs.py:1324-1359, reads back).

REFUTED / already mitigated parts: (1) 'the desk absorbs any burst' — the only unpaced burst in the product is panic's 24 datagrams, and HANDOVER §4a (line 114) verified 24/24 muted on the real X32 (FW 4.13, wired) and confirmed visually. Every other write goes through the token-bucket limiter (policy.py:375-396), and bulk restore uses `conn.slash()` which awaits the desk's '/' echo per line with retries (desk.py:1312-1331, connection.py:542-554) — exactly the flow control transport.md §6.6/§10 prescribes. (2) 'dump over Wi-Fi loses sections -> restore_plan rewrites those sections from a holey snapshot' — wrong: dump retries each /node (finding itself concedes missing==0), missing paths are tracked in DeskState.missing (nodes.py:727-748), and restore_plan SKIPS any section absent from the snapshot (`want is None: continue`, nodes.py:1214-1216); it never writes a section it does not have. (3) A lost CFS notch SET self-heals: VERIFY is an acoustic closed loop (cfs.py:1200-1252) — the band does not decay, the controller deepens, the next SET lands at -6 and desk state and bookkeeping re-converge; worst case is ~decay_verify_s of extra ringing during an attended ring-out plus 3 dB over-cut, or (if the -9 write is the lost one) ABORT + 6 dB master back-off with the report showing -9 where the desk has -6. `existing` is re-read from the desk at the next preflight (cfs.py:886), so the bookkeeping error does not persist across sessions. (4) set_rta_source does verify via /-stat/rtasource read-back (meters.py:925-937).

Would it bite at a gig? On the documented primary deployment (README:289, wired Windows PC on the desk LAN; GIG_CHECKLIST uses Wi-Fi only for the tablet->PC dashboard over HTTP) inbound loss of ~24-60 B unicast datagrams is effectively nil and was measured 24/24. The residual risk needs the secondary Termux-tablet-over-Wi-Fi OSC host (README:806-811, itself flagged unconfirmed) plus a loss event on a specific datagram; 802.11 unicast has link-layer ARQ so per-datagram loss is typically well under 1% except on congested venue Wi-Fi. When it does happen the consequence is audible, not silent (the wedge that prompted 'kill it' keeps howling; the untamed ring keeps ringing with the operator standing at the desk during an attended ring-out) and panic is idempotent — press it again. The entire X32 remote ecosystem (X32-Edit, Mixing Station on Wi-Fi tablets) is fire-and-forget SET and is used at gigs daily. Net: a genuine test-fidelity hole worth closing (add a seedable `inbound_loss_rate` to FakeDesk; give panic a post-send GET/`/node` read-back of the 24 `mix/on` leaves and report `unconfirmed: [...]` — costs ~10 ms after the mutes are already on the wire, so it does not slow the kill; read back the BACKOFF master like `_restore_master` does), but not something that lies to the operator on the wired rig this project ships for. Severity low, not medium.

## E72. [low] (fakedesk-fidelity, partial) Every input channel carries programme (≈-12 dBFS) that follows its fader and mute; there is no such thing as an unplugged input, and meter silence is 1e-5.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:930-941 (_strip_level: 0.25×wobble for every strip, SILENCE_LIN 1e-5 when muted/fader<=0; pre_fade variant is 0.25 for ALL 72 strips regardless of source, head-amp gain or whether anything is connected), :956-970 channel words of /meters/0, /1, /13 follow mix/fader and mix/on. tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:283-288 asserts ch1 > 0.1 and 'muted: silence level' for a CHANNEL meter; test_server_tools.py:550-559 get_meters shapes only.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/provision.py:557-606 discover_mics decides 'include' from unmuted+send+physical preamp only (no meter evidence) — HANDOVER §4b: 7 candidates with 1 mic plugged in; src/x32mcp/server.py:1420-1461 get_meters('channels') documents '-90 = silence' and is the tool the model would use to answer 'is the vocal mic live?'; meters.lin_to_db floor -90 (meters.py:125-130).

**Reality:** meters.md §2.2 (verbatim desk capture): idle input pre-fade = 9.6e-6 (-100.35 dBFS), muted post-fade = exactly 10^(-128/20) = 3.98e-7; §4.1 'Silence is not 0.0 … expect ~1e-5 … 4e-7'; §3: /meters/1 [0-31] are the channel (input) meters and /meters/6 word 0 is 'post gain/trim (pre-fade)'. An open XLR with +44.5 dB of SM58 gain (HANDOVER §4a ch 4) reads room noise around -60..-50 dBFS; an unpatched card channel reads the -100/-128 floor. HANDOVER §4b: 'Cross-checking candidates against actual meter activity would catch it (an unplugged input reads near-silent, a live mic picks up room noise)' — impossible to develop against this fake, where all 32 inputs look identical and live.

**On a real desk:** discover_mics keeps including line inputs, spare channels and unplugged stage-box channels as 'stage mics' (7 for 1 at M7), so preflight passes on buses with no open mic and ring_out raises a monitor master step by step to the target with nothing to detect — then a mic is plugged in hot. get_meters tested only against the fake cannot tell the model whether a channel meter is pre- or post-fader, so 'ch 5 shows -90, the mic is dead' may just mean the fader is down.

**Offline test:** FakeDesk input model: per head-amp 'connected' flag + ambient level (default: nothing connected → pre-fade 9.6e-6; connected mic → -55 dBFS + gain; muted/fader-down post-fade → 3.98e-7 exactly); channel meters in /meters/0,/1,/13 pre-fader, bus/main post-fader. Tests: discover_mics on a bus where ch1 (mic connected) and ch2 (nothing connected) are both routed must include only ch1 once the meter cross-check exists — today both are included; get_meters must report -100 vs -128 distinctly (floor -128, not -90).

These are human-in-loop, not automatic, so discover_mics still reports wrong state at a gig → medium per the rubric, not high.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — What holds: the FakeDesk really has no concept of an unplugged/idle input. fakedesk.py:930-941 (_strip_level) gives every one of the 70/72 strips 0.25×wobble (≈ -12 dBFS) post-fader whenever mix/on=1 and fader>0, SILENCE_LIN=1e-5 (fakedesk.py:100) otherwise, and a constant 0.25 pre-fade for /meters/6 word 0 regardless of source, head-amp gain (only a static 'gain': 24.0 default at :134) or whether anything is connected; fakedesk.py:956-961 make the /meters/0, /1, /13 channel words track /ch/NN/mix/fader and mix/on. tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:283-288 certifies exactly that belief (ch1 > 0.1 unmuted; ch2 < 1e-4 once muted, citing 'meters.md §6.3') and test_server_tools.py:550-558 checks get_meters shapes only. meters.md §2.2/§4.1/§6.3 confirm the real desk's floors are 9.6e-6 (-100 dBFS, idle input pre-fade) and exactly 3.98e-7 (-128 dBFS, muted post-fade), which the fake collapses to one 1e-5 value. What does not hold or is overstated: (1) 'code depends on it' is indirect — discover_mics never reads a meter, so its correctness does not depend on the fake's meter model; the over-inclusion is the already-tracked HANDOVER §4b item and is the designed 'open-loop' heuristic (BRIEF.md:78, provision.py:27-34), and the tool contract disclaims it: server.py:1618-1621 "'include' is a suggestion — confirm it with the user; nothing is unmuted", with the server instructions (server.py:132) requiring the open-mic list to be confirmed before feedback_watch/ring_out and ring_out itself behind a Tier-2 confirmation. Automix.c's use of /meters/1 to wake faded-down channels strongly implies pre-fader, so the fake's post-fader model and test_fakedesk.py:288 are plausibly wrong, but it is UNCONFIRMED either way and no product logic branches on the tap: get_meters (server.py:1420-1461) is a Tier-0 passthrough and its docstring claims neither pre nor post; CFS uses /meters/15 only (cfs.py:508). (3) 'get_meters must report -100 vs -128 distinctly' is cosmetic: lin_to_db's -90 floor (meters.py:125-130) still cleanly separates a live mic's room noise (≈-60..-50 dBFS) from nothing (≤ -90); no operator decision needs -100 vs -128. Net: a real fake-fidelity gap worth fixing so the §4b meter cross-check can be built and tested offline, but today it produces no wrong write and no automated action on garbage; the only gig-visible symptom is the known, disclaimed, human-filtered noisy candidate list. Downgraded to low.

Net: worth adding insert exclusivity + /-insert leaves to FakeDesk so the provision.py:412 'is also inserted on' branch and a post-write reconcile become testable (and to probe restore_snapshot's per-strip insert write ordering, a separate angle), but the gig-time scenario described is already caught by the re-plan + payload-bound token. Downgraded to low.

## E75. [low] (fakedesk-fidelity, confirmed) The console's RTA and its prefs belong to the server for the duration (and after): nobody was using auto-gain, RMS, a dynamic 'selected channel' source or Solo Priority, so overwriting them and never restoring them costs nothing.

**Encoded at:** FakeDesk has no operator and no second client: /-prefs/rta/* start at fixed defaults (fakedesk.py:159-160) and nothing but the server ever writes them; tests assert autogain_cleared/detector_set_peak as achievements (test_server_tools/test_cfs rta dict) and never that anything is put back.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/meters.py:888-923 set_rta_source overwrites source (fixed strip), pos, options bit 5, autogain=0, det=PEAK on every arm and on get_rta(target); src/x32mcp/nodes.py:1204-1212 restore_plan never restores -prefs sections, and cfs _finish/stop restores the master fader only — the RTA prefs are left as CFS needed them.
