> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (low)** — Code citations check out: FakeDesk._h_slash (src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1012-1021) parses with our own parse_node_line and echoes the datagram unconditionally (docstring :22-25 says so explicitly); tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:212-213 pins 'unknown node still echoed, nothing applied'; Desk.restore (src/x32mcp/desk.py:1312-1341) counts a returned conn.slash() (= echo received) as `written`, never re-reads or re-diffs, and server.restore_snapshot (server.py:1260-1266) reports 'written/lines section(s) written'; tests/integration/test_desk.py:447 asserts failed==[] and lines==written. restore_plan (nodes.py:1201-1227) does emit one '/' line per differing section for fx/N/par (64 fields), */grp (%bitmaps), config/userrout/in (32) / out (16), headamp/NNN, dca/N, config/linkcfg, config/talk/A. The committed test (cf11e8b, tests/integration/test_assumptions_restore.py::test_restore_reports_a_line_the_desk_echoed_but_did_not_apply) exists and fails exactly as described (lines=1 written=1 failed=[] while /fx/5/par/27 still -9.0). transport.md §6.6 does document the echo only as flow control, scales_params.md §4.10 does flag the emulator's XslashSetPerInt %-bitmap bug, fx_routing_scenes.md §1.6 does show X32SetScene sending /fx/N/par as one typed ,f×64 message, transport.md §10 does mark the 512 B ceiling UNCONFIRMED, HANDOVER §4a's live restore was 3 sections with a clean diff afterwards.

But the 'reality' argument that makes this a real-desk failure is overstated and partly wrong. (1) 'No source shows a real desk accepting these shapes through /' and 'the one tool proven against real desks avoids exactly the path restore relies on': Maillot's X32DeskRestore.c (a real-desk tool, cited in the research base at meters.md:21; change-log v0.91 'replacing longer parsing commands by the use of "/" X32 commands', adapted to FW 3.04) restores by reading each saved /node line and sending `/ ,s <line>`, waiting for the echo and ignoring it (X32DeskRestore.c:403-430) — and the node list it round-trips (X32ds_node.h sc_node[], written by X32DeskSave -s) includes /ch/NN/grp (bitmaps), /fx/1..8/par (64 dB tokens), /dca/N, /headamp/000..127, /config/mute|linkcfg|talk/A|routing/*. So the exact mechanism and almost every line shape restore_plan emits IS what the established real-desk restore tool does; X32SetScene's typed conversion is an older/different tool, and the research never says it 'deliberately' avoids '/'. The DOC (transport.md §6.6, CONFIRMED) also describes '/' generically as taking node-reply text. (2) The truncation angle is weak: restore_plan renders unpadded, so a 64-token /fx/5/par line is ~140-260 B, not ~400 B, comfortably under even the UNCONFIRMED 512 B ceiling. (3) The XslashSetPerInt bug is Maillot's emulator, not the desk; real-desk /showdump and scene files print %bitmaps and DeskRestore feeds them straight back.

What survives: restore's success figure is genuinely unverified — the echo is only documented as flow control, both our fake and Maillot's emulator echo lines they could not apply, the fake can never reject a line our renderer produces because it parses with the same code, and the FW-4 /config/userrout/in (32 tokens) and /out (16 tokens) lines are in no real-desk tool's list and were not among the 3 sections restored live. A post-restore re-dump/diff (or reporting 'unverified') is a reasonable fix and the proposed FakeDesk 'slash_reject' hook is a fair offline test. But there is no evidence any emitted line is actually rejected by a real desk, and positive external evidence that fx/par, grp bitmaps, headamp, dca and config lines are accepted this way, so the headline gig failure ('GEQ notches not restored while tool says N/N written', 'DCA membership re-assigned wrongly') is speculative. Downgraded to PARTIAL / low (would rise to medium only if a FW-4 desk is shown to ignore a '/' userrout or other emitted line — a one-minute live check).

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The finding's load-bearing claim — that no real-desk source shows the `/ ,s <node line>` path accepting 64-token `/fx/N/par` in dB, `%` bitmaps on `/ch/NN/grp`, `/dca/N`, `/headamp/NNN`, `/config/linkcfg`, `/config/talk/A`, and that "the one tool proven against real desks (X32SetScene/fxparse.c) avoids exactly the path restore relies on" — is wrong. Maillot ships TWO real-desk tools that do precisely what Desk.restore does: (1) X32DeskRestore.c (changelog 0.91: "cleaned the code, replacing longer parsing commands by the use of \"/\" X32 commands"; 0.93 "adapted to FW ver 3.04") reads the node list in X32ds_node.h — which includes "/ch/01/grp" (line 119), "/dca/1".."/dca/8" (+/config), "/fx/1/par".."/fx/8/par" (1941–1958), "/headamp/000".. (2033), "/config/linkcfg" (64), "/config/talk/A" (68) — saves the desk's own `/node` text and restores it by `Xsprint(s_buf,0,'s',"/"); Xsprint(..,",s"); Xsprint(..,l_read); SEND_TO; RPOLL; recvfrom(...) // manage the echo of the command from X32, ignoring the answer` (X32DeskRestore.c:409–421), i.e. echo-as-flow-control, no read-back, BSIZE 512; (2) X32_Command.c `-s` (v1.31 "Added 's' flag to read/send scene/snippets/tidbits/X32node lines from file", lines 416–428) sends arbitrary scene/snippet lines through `/` and waits for the echo — this is cited in the repo's own research (mcp_sdk.md:967, transport.md:353). restore_plan re-emits the desk's own node tokens (snapshot values are the parsed node text, e.g. '0.0' for GEQ par), which is exactly the X32DeskSave→X32DeskRestore round trip. The XslashSetPerInt `%` bug cited from scales_params.md §4.10 is explicitly an EMULATOR (X32.c) bug with the instruction to test the emulator with plain ints; it says nothing about the console, whose own scene/snippet files are `%` bitmaps loaded through the same text grammar. X32SetScene using typed `,f×64` is an alternative, not evidence that `/` fails. And HANDOVER §4a records a live FW-4.13 restore: "restore wrote 3 sections in 9 ms, and the diff afterwards was clean" — the `/` write path demonstrably applies on the target desk. The committed failing test (cf11e8b test_restore_reports_a_line_the_desk_echoed_but_did_not_apply) manufactures the failure by monkey-patching FakeDesk._apply_node_text to drop `/fx/5/par`; it models no documented desk behaviour, so it proves only the tautology that an unverified write is unverified. FakeDesk's behaviour (parse the line with the node grammar, apply, echo verbatim regardless — fakedesk.py:1012–1021) matches DOC 4591–4593, the emulator (X32.c 3769–3771) and what Maillot's real-desk tools rely on, so per the brief this part is REFUTED.

What survives, at low severity: (a) Desk.restore (desk.py:1319–1333) equates echo with success and restore_snapshot (server.py:1260–1266) prints "N/N section(s) written" without a post-restore diff; an echo proves receipt, not that every token landed (e.g. a value snapped, a trailing token dropped on a firmware whose node has fewer fields). This is the same contract X32DeskRestore accepts, the wording says "written" not "verified", diff_snapshot is one tool call away (and was run live in M5), and a lost echo errs safe (line reported failed). (b) `/config/userrout/in` (32 tokens) and `/config/userrout/out` are FW-4 nodes with no real-desk `/`-write precedent in any Maillot tool (X32ds_node.h predates them); they only enter a plan if routing changed between snapshot and restore, which the ring-out undo flow never does. Neither rises to "tool reports wrong state at a gig": the concrete failure the finding predicts (GEQ notches left in after undo while the tool says N/N) has no supporting evidence and is contradicted by X32DeskRestore restoring /fx/N/par this exact way on real consoles. Reasonable hardening (append an automatic scoped diff to restore_snapshot's result and report still_different; optionally a FakeDesk slash_reject/slash_max_bytes knob to exercise it) is a nice-to-have, not a defect of the assumed-world class the brief is hunting.

## E85. [low] (scales-nodes, confirmed) Every enum token the desk will ever print is in device.yaml, so it is safe for the parser to keep an unknown token verbatim while the renderer refuses it.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/nodes.py:339 parse_token returns an unknown enum token verbatim (no error, not None); nodes.py:384 format_token → enum_to_index raises; tests/test_nodes.py:423-425 enshrines BOTH halves (`parse_token(color,'NEWTOKEN') == 'NEWTOKEN'` and `pytest.raises(NodeParseError): format_token(color,'NEWTOKEN')`); FakeDesk can only ever print tokens from the same yaml. Enum lists never seen from a real console per scales_params.md §11.2: dyn_ratio `10 20 100`, hpslope `12 18`, filter_type LC6…, send_type `IN/LC <-EQ EQ-> GRP`, eq_type_mtx BU6…LR24, routing_aes/out (`P161-8`, `AUX1-6/Mon`, `AuxIN1-6/TB`, `AUX/CR`…), talk_source, mono_mode `LCR`, most fx types.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/nodes.py:1227 restore_plan renders every picked section in one list comprehension with no try/except; src/x32mcp/desk.py:1319 calls it unguarded → one unknown token in one CHANGED section raises NodeParseError out of Desk.restore and NOTHING is restored. HANDOVER §4a's '0 missing, 0 unparsed fields … retires the FW 4.x node-text risk' counted None fields — an unknown enum spelling is a verbatim string, not None, so that sweep could not see it (nor a same-typed column swap, nor `/` write acceptance).

**Reality:** transport.md §6.3 'Token count is firmware-dependent' and the research repeatedly flags emulator-vs-desk spelling drift (`EXP` vs `EXP4`, `Lcut` vs `LCut`, `10.0` vs `10` Q, glued `45%`); the routing/RTA token tables come from DOC 4.06 + emulator, the desk is FW 4.13. Probe: `/ch/05/dyn … 10.0 …` (ratio spelled with a decimal) parses to dyn/ratio='10.0'; restore_plan(target, live) → `NodeParseError: ch:dyn/ratio: unknown token '10.0'`.

**On a real desk:** At the gig the operator asks for the undo; restore_snapshot returns an INTERNAL error and writes zero lines because ch 12's compressor ratio (or an AES50 routing block, or a colour added in a firmware update) prints a spelling we do not list. The pre-write safety net is gone exactly when needed; diff_snapshot still works, so the state looks inspectable but not restorable.

**Offline test:** Committed failing test (cf11e8b): tests/test_assumptions_nodes.py::test_restore_plan_survives_an_enum_token_device_yaml_does_not_know. Fix: make format_token pass an unknown str through verbatim for `enum` (symmetry with parse), and make restore_plan/Desk.restore skip-and-report a section it cannot render instead of aborting; add a dump-time WARNING listing verbatim-kept tokens so a real-desk sweep actually surfaces spelling drift (and re-run it on the FW 4.13 desk).

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (medium)** — Mechanism, citations and absence of a fallback all check out; the committed test fails today exactly as described. Caveats: (1) the tool error code is BAD_ARGUMENT, not INTERNAL (NodeParseError subclasses ValueError and server._error_dict maps ValueError→BAD_ARGUMENT) — immaterial to the outcome (ok:false, 0 lines written); (2) the 'reality' evidence is weaker than stated: the spelling-drift examples in transport.md §6.3 / scales_params.md §4.7 (`EXP` vs `EXP4`, ` Lcut`, glued `45%`) are emulator-side slips and the research says 'Desk output is unaffected'; device.yaml already uses the desk spellings; the `10.0` ratio probe is hypothetical, and §6.3's 'firmware-dependent' sentence is about token COUNT. No real-desk snapshot exists in the repo to check for verbatim-kept tokens. Nonetheless the assumption is genuinely unverified for FW 4.13 (tables sourced from DOC 4.06 + emulator; scales_params §11.2 lists only a subset of enum tokens as seen from a real console), the parser's own comment at nodes.py:339 anticipates 'newer firmware?' tokens, the FakeDesk renders via render_node_line from the same yaml so can never emit one, and the HANDOVER §4a '0 unparsed' sweep counts None values only (parse_node_line sets None only on NodeParseError; unknown enums return the string) so it could not have detected this class. The consequence — one unlisted token in one changed section aborts the entire undo with zero writes — is a spurious whole-tool failure at a gig, i.e. medium per the rubric; no wrong write occurs.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — Mechanism CONFIRMED, real-world trigger speculative, consequence bounded -> PARTIAL, downgraded to low.

What holds up (reproduced on HEAD a408a2a):
- src/x32mcp/nodes.py:330-339 parse_token keeps an unknown enum token verbatim (comment literally says 'newer firmware? — keep verbatim'); nodes.py:381-384 format_token -> enum_to_index raises NodeParseError; tests/test_nodes.py:423-425 pins both halves. nodes.py:1227 restore_plan renders every picked section in one list comprehension, desk.py:1319 calls it unguarded, so the exception escapes before the write loop: 0 lines written, including unrelated sections. My repro: target /ch/05/dyn with ratio token '10.0' + a changed /ch/05/mix -> restore_plan raises 'ch:dyn/ratio: unknown token '10.0'; expected one of 1.1 … 100' and the /ch/05/mix undo is lost too. Only production caller of format_token/render_node_line outside the FakeDesk is restore_plan, so the blast radius is exactly restore_snapshot (the undo).
- The HANDOVER §4a claim '0 missing, 0 unparsed … retires the FW 4.x node-text risk' is indeed blind to this class: parse_node_line (nodes.py:476-486) only produces None on NodeParseError, and an unknown enum never raises, so an enum spelling drift on the FW 4.13 desk would have sailed through that sweep. The live restore in §4a wrote only 3 sections, so enum rendering was barely exercised on real hardware. FakeDesk renders from the same device.yaml, so no test can produce an unknown token today; the proposer's failing test (cf11e8b tests/test_assumptions_nodes.py::test_restore_plan_survives_an_enum_token_device_yaml_does_not_know) is a fair offline pin.
- Firmware precedent that enum lists do grow: FW 4.0 added UIN*/UOUT* routing tokens (fx_routing_scenes.md §4.x, device.yaml:125-132), and /config/routing IS in the restore plan (family 'config' not excluded, nodes.py:111).

What does not hold up / why downgraded:
- The cited 'reality' is overstated. docs/research does NOT flag the enum spellings as UNCONFIRMED: transport.md §6.3 (l.443) lists dyn ratio '… 10 20 100', filter '… 10.0' etc. as VERIFIED, and scales_params.md §11.2 (l.682-711) says every list was re-read from X32.c, X32SetScene.h (which parses real-desk .scn dumps) and the PDF and 'all agree'; real-console dyn lines show ratio '3.0'/'2.0' (scales_params.md l.435), matching device.yaml:108. The drifts the finding quotes (EXP vs EXP4, glued 45%, Lcut) are emulator typos where the desk spelling is the known-good one, and case drift is already absorbed (parse is case-insensitive, nodes.py:335-338). The '10.0' ratio probe is invented, not observed. 'Token count is firmware-dependent' (transport.md l.460) is about a missing trailing panFollow token, which the positional parser already tolerates.
- Error class is wrong in the finding: NodeParseError subclasses ValueError (nodes.py:124), so server._error_dict (server.py:289) returns BAD_ARGUMENT with a message naming the exact field and the accepted tokens, not INTERNAL. No wrong write occurs; diff_snapshot still works; a scoped restore (scope='ch.6', 'bus', …) that avoids the offending section succeeds, so there is an at-the-gig workaround, albeit an awkward one under pressure.
- Net: for Jim's FW 4.13 desk there is no evidence any restorable-family enum prints outside the DOC-4.06/X32SetScene lists (no enum additions are known between 4.06 and 4.13), so this is unlikely to bite at this gig; it is a cheap robustness fix to the undo path (pass unknown str through in format_token for enum, and make restore_plan/Desk.restore skip-and-report an unrenderable section instead of aborting) plus a one-line dump-time warning for verbatim-kept tokens so the next real-desk sweep can actually retire the risk. Worth doing, but 'medium' overstates the demonstrated gig consequence.

## E86. [low] (scales-nodes, partial) An FX slot's 64 parameters persist across a type change and a type load is instantaneous, so `set type` immediately followed by `write par`/`read par` is sound.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1082-1092 `_side_effects` has no branch for `/fx/N/type` (raws kept), and :537 defaults EVERY slot's par to raw 0.5 ('0 dB on a GEQ') regardless of effect, so a freshly 'loaded' GEQ2 is flat by coincidence of the fixture; no test loads a type and checks parameters were re-initialised or delayed.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/nodes.py:1174-1199 restore order writes `/fx/N` (type) then, several to hundreds of lines later, `/fx/N/par` with no settle or read-back; desk.py:1389-1401 set_fx_type only drops the par cache; provision.apply_setup (provision.py:512-530) loads GEQ2 then immediately inserts and validates (the validate half already failed live: HANDOVER §4b GEQ_VALIDATION_FAILED).

**Reality:** fx_routing_scenes.md §2.2: X32CopyFX.c `FXdef[]` are per-type 'real default values' captured from a desk (GEQ2/GEQ rows all `0.0`) — selecting an effect loads that effect's defaults; §6.4 quotes DOC fn.39-41 'the load/save/copy operation is not necessarily fully completed when the status is returned' for the analogous DSP reload; HANDOVER §4b/REVIEW_BRIEF §5 document the same read-after-write race on insert/on. Whether a `/fx/N/par` line landing tens of ms after a type change survives the DSP swap is UNCONFIRMED and untested.

**On a real desk:** Restoring a snapshot whose slot 5 was GEQ2-with-notches onto a desk where slot 5 now holds DES2: type write, then par write; if the effect finishes loading after the par line, the slot comes up flat — notches silently gone (and per the echo finding, reported written). Conversely the fake lets a −9 dB notch survive DES2→GEQ2, so tests around 'reuse an existing GEQ' see cuts a real desk would have wiped.

**Offline test:** Committed failing test (cf11e8b): tests/integration/test_assumptions_restore.py::test_loading_an_effect_type_loads_its_defaults_like_the_desk (−9.0 persists across DES2→GEQ2 on the fake; a desk gives 0.0). Then give FakeDesk an optional `fx_load_delay_ms` during which par writes are dropped/overwritten by defaults, and assert restore/apply_setup settle or verify (they do not today).

> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (medium)** — Citations check out and the fixture gap is real, but the claimed real-desk failure rests on the part the finder itself marks UNCONFIRMED, one code citation is overstated, and half the impact is the already-known §4b race.

CONFIRMED: (1) src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1082-1092 `_side_effects` handles only /-prefs/rta/{source,pos}, /-action/goscene and scene fields — nothing for /fx/N/type; :536-537 defaults every slot's par/* to raw 0.5 regardless of effect. `FakeDesk.set` goes through `_commit`→`_side_effects` (:432-441, :815-820), so the finder's committed test (wt/assumptions-scales-nodes cf11e8b, tests/integration/test_assumptions_restore.py:68-80) exercises the real write path and fails as stated (−9.0 dB survives DES2→GEQ2; expected 0.0). (2) docs/research/fx_routing_scenes.md §2.2 (line 239) verifier note does say X32CopyFX.c:99-130 FXdef[] are "real default values" captured from a desk with GEQ2/GEQ rows `0.0 …`; §6.4 (line 565) quotes DOC fn.39-41 "load/save/copy operation is not necessarily fully completed when the status is returned" verbatim — but that is about /load,/save,/copy, which the finder honestly calls "analogous"; HANDOVER §4b (lines 181-183) documents the insert/on read-after-write race → false GEQ_VALIDATION_FAILED. (3) Code: nodes.py:1174-1188 gives /fx/N (root → kind "mix") and /fx/N/par the same (fam 8, strip 0, rank 0) key because fx is not in d.strips, so order is pure sweep index: 8 type lines, 4 source lines, 8 par lines; Desk.restore (desk.py:1312-1341) writes them back-to-back through conn.slash with echo-only ack at up to 50/s (device.yaml:733), no settle, no read-back, and server.restore_snapshot (server.py:1240-1266) reports written/lines from echoes only. provision.apply_setup (provision.py:512-530) does set_fx_type → set_insert → validate_ringout_eqs with no settle. No fallback missed.

My own probe (worktree wt/verify-fx-type-defaults-restore, commit dae7ded, tests/integration/test_verify_fx_type_defaults.py): patch FakeDesk so a type change loads defaults (all 64 par → 0.5) either synchronously or 150 ms later. Synchronous: restore of a GEQ2-with-−9 dB-notch snapshot onto a slot now holding DES2 PASSES (type-then-par order is correct for a desk that resets on load). Deferred 150 ms: restore returns 2/2 written, failed=[], slot type GEQ2, band 27 = +0.0 dB — notch silently gone while the tool reports success. So the restore failure exists only if the desk applies the effect's defaults asynchronously after acknowledging the type write — exactly the UNCONFIRMED part; the research-supported part (defaults are loaded) does not by itself break restore.

NOT CONFIRMED / overstated: "several to hundreds of lines later" is wrong — par follows type within the fx block (adjacent when only one slot differs, ≤12 lines in a full restore), which if anything tightens the race; desk.set_fx_type dropping the par cache (desk.py:1400) is the correct response to a defaults load, not a dependency on the wrong belief; no existing test was found that changes type and relies on cuts persisting (the 'reuse an existing GEQ' converse is speculative); the apply_setup validate-after-load race is the known HANDOVER §4b item the brief lists as a calibration example (and is separately under review in wt/verify-fx-type-load-latency).

Net: valid fixture-fidelity finding (FakeDesk cannot exhibit per-type default loading or load latency, so restore/apply_setup's no-settle-after-type-load path is uncertified), real-desk impact plausible (same race class already bit this desk on insert/on; an FX program swap is unlikely to be faster) but unverified. Severity kept at medium because if it occurs the restore tool reports success while ring-out notches are gone (feedback returns at the gig) and nothing mitigates it; downgrade to low if a live check shows /fx/N/par written immediately after /fx/N/type survives.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — What holds: the FakeDesk fidelity observation is accurate. src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1082-1092 (_side_effects) has no /fx/N/type branch, so the 64 raw floats survive a type change, and :537 answers raw 0.5 for every unset par in every slot regardless of effect. A real X32 very likely re-initialises a slot to the effect's defaults on a type load (X32CopyFX.c:99-130 FXdef[] 'real default values respective of each effects', v1.20 changelog), so the fake is more permissive than reality here and a one-line fix (reset /fx/N/par/01..64 on a type change) would stop any future test from depending on persistence. That is worth doing, but it is a latent fidelity gap, not a defect that bites.

What does not hold:
1. The claimed gig failure (restore writes /fx/5 GEQ2 then /fx/5/par, the par line is lost to a still-loading DSP, notches silently gone) is contradicted by the primary research source's own real-desk tooling. Maillot's X32SetScene — the tool people actually use to push .scn files into real X32s — does exactly this: SetSceneParse.c:2511-2516/2540-2545 send '/fx/N/type ,i' and the very next scene lines (2528-2534/2547-2552) send '/fx/N/par ,fff…64' fire-and-forget with the default Xdelay = 1 ms (X32SetScene.c 'default is 1ms between commands', SendDataToX32 macro SetSceneParse.c:69-78) and no read-back. The console's own scene recall is the same order. x32mcp's restore is strictly more conservative: desk.py:1323-1327 writes one line per rate-limiter slot and conn.slash (connection.py:542-554) awaits the desk's verbatim '/' echo before the next line goes out. The DOC fn.39-41 quote ('load/save/copy not necessarily completed') is about /load, /save, /copy file/library operations (fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4), not a /fx/N/type parameter set; the finder themself marks the race UNCONFIRMED. No evidence supports modelling an fx_load_delay_ms window that drops par writes.
2. set_fx_type (desk.py:1389-1401) dropping only the par cache is correct under either model of reality; nothing reads or writes pars immediately after it. The only product caller is provision.apply_setup (provision.py:512-519), which writes NO parameters after the load — it relies on a freshly loaded GEQ2 being flat, which is exactly what the finder says the real desk does (FXdef GEQ2 row all 0.0). GEQ notch writes happen later in a separate ring_out/feedback_watch tool call, seconds to minutes afterwards. The validate-immediately-after-set_insert race in apply_setup is the already-documented HANDOVER §4b GEQ_VALIDATION_FAILED item, not a new finding.
3. 'Tests around reuse see cuts a real desk would have wiped': reuse in plan_setup (provision.py:457-463) is by definition a slot that already holds a GEQ — no type change occurs. grep of tests/ shows no test that changes type and expects params to persist; test_apply_setup_validates_and_is_idempotent (tests/integration/test_cfs.py:141-153) asserts flat after DES2->GEQ2, which matches real-desk defaults. The committed failing test (cf11e8b test_loading_an_effect_type_loads_its_defaults_like_the_desk) only demonstrates the fake's behaviour; it exercises no product code.
4. The FakeDesk matches the reference emulator here: Maillot X32.c:3555-3558 (case FXTYP1/FXTYP2) just stores the enum and does not touch pars either; docs/research is silent on type-change parameter semantics, so this is not code depending on an UNCONFIRMED item without fallback.
Residual real risk is a contrived restore edge (snapshot and live par text identical while types differ -> restore_plan at nodes.py:1210-1216 skips the par line and a real desk's default-load would flatten it); different effects print pars in different display units so this essentially requires GEQ2<->TEQ2 with identical settings. Cosmetic/latent -> low.

5. Gig realism: to be included a channel must also be unmuted AND sending >= -40 dB to the monitor bus (provision.py:590-591). An engineer does not turn up a channel routed to an input that does not exist; the only plausible trigger is a stale scene from a show where a stage box was present. Result: a spurious candidate the operator declines, not a wrong write.

Net: a real unmodelled assumption (model preamp count / AES50 link state never consulted) worth a note, but cosmetic-to-low in consequence and already covered by the §4b follow-up. ## E88. [low] (scales-nodes, confirmed) Anything not in `-show/-stat/-prefs/-action` is safe and intended to be written back by a restore; a param's tier is irrelevant to restore.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/nodes.py:111 `_RESTORE_EXCLUDED_FAMILIES = {show, stat, prefs, action}`; tests/test_nodes.py:816 only asserts those three prefixes are absent; device.yaml:492-531 marks `/config/solo/*`, `/config/talk/*`, `talk/A|B/*`, `/config/mono/*` tier 0 with the comment 'read-only in v1 (BRIEF §8)' yet they sit in restorable `config` node sections (device.yaml:679-683).

**Code depends on it at:** nodes.py:1201-1227 restore_plan never consults `spec.tier`; desk.py:1326 writes the lines via conn.slash, bypassing Policy's per-address tier checks entirely (only the single restore confirmation applies).

**Reality:** Physical desk semantics: `/config/mono/mode` LR+M↔LCR changes the main-bus pan law for the whole PA; `/config/solo/level|source|dim…` and `/config/talk/*` drive the engineer's cue wedge/IEM and talkback routing (scales_params.md §10). The descriptor author classified them read-only precisely because v1 should not touch them; restore writes them anyway whenever they differ from the snapshot (e.g. the engineer changed solo mode or talkback destination during the show).

**On a real desk:** An undo scoped 'whole desk' flips the operator's monitor/solo/talkback settings and possibly the LR+M/LCR mode mid-show — changes nobody asked for, applied under a token that previewed '… N more'.

**Offline test:** Unit test: build target/live differing only in `/config/solo` and `/config/mono`; assert restore_plan emits nothing (or requires an explicit `include_readonly=True`). Fails today (both lines emitted). Fix: skip sections whose every field is tier 0, or list restorable sections explicitly in device.yaml.

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (medium)** — Every citation checks out and there is no fallback the claimant missed. (2) tests/test_nodes.py:816 is literally `assert not any(p.startswith(("/-prefs", "/-show", "/-stat")) for p in paths)` — the only exclusion assertion. (3) device.yaml:490 comments "solo / monitor section — read-only in v1 (BRIEF §8)", 491-507 declare every `solo/*` param `tier: 0`; 508 "talkback — read-only in v1", 509-518 `talk/*` tier 0; 519-520 `mono/mode`/`mono/link` tier 0; yet device.yaml:680-684 list `/config/solo`, `/config/talk`, `/config/talk/A|B`, `/config/mono` as `family: config` node sections, which restore_plan treats as restorable (descriptor.py:288 documents `tier: int  # 0 read-only`). (4) desk.py:1312-1334 `Desk.restore` writes each plan line with `await self._conn.slash(line)` (line 1326) after only `acquire_write()` — no tier lookup; the only gate is the single Tier-2 `restore_snapshot` confirmation in server.py:1240-1259, whose preview is `describe_changes(changes[:15]) + "… N more"`, and diff_states emits changes in sweep order where config nodes (device.yaml:662-684) come after all strips/headamp/fx, so solo/talk/mono changes fall into the truncated tail on any non-trivial whole-desk restore. (5) I reproduced the proposed offline test against HEAD a408a2a: target=full_state(d,7), live differing only in /config/solo/chmode, /config/mono/mode, /config/talk/A/destmap → restore_plan returns ['/config/solo 0.0 LRPFL 18.0 PFL AFL PFL ON OFF ON -20 ON OFF ON 0.3 ON OFF ON', '/config/talk/A -0.5 OFF ON %010010000101011010', '/config/mono LCR OFF'] while d.tier_for() reports 0 for all three addresses. So the descriptor's declared read-only params are written by restore today. No mitigating code exists: no restore-exclusion list in device.yaml, Desk._write itself never refuses tier 0 (only tier>=2), and DESIGN §9 explicitly includes the whole `config` family in restore. Severity medium is appropriate: the values written are a prior real desk state (not garbage) and sit behind a Tier-2 confirmation, but they are unrequested writes to the engineer's solo/talkback/mono-mode settings that the descriptor itself classifies read-only, hidden in the preview tail.

Nothing in research/HANDOVER says writing them is wrong or unsafe; HANDOVER M5 restore on the real desk was clean. The LR+M↔LCR flip is theoretical — nobody toggles /config/mono/mode mid-show, and if it did differ from the snapshot, restoring it is arguably the correct undo. (5) What survives: a reasonable UX/design nit — restore has no equivalent of the desk's Talkback/Solo/Configuration safes, and because config nodes are last in sweep order their changes land in the '… N more' tail of the 15-line preview (server.py:1249). Worth an include/exclude option or surfacing config-family changes first, but it is not a wrong write, not a safety issue, and not an emulator-vs-reality divergence. Downgraded to low.

## E89. [low] (scales-nodes, confirmed) A name is 12 *characters* of arbitrary Unicode; what we send is what the desk stores and prints back.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/osc.py:82 encodes strings UTF-8; desk.py:1168-1169 truncates to `_NAME_MAX=12` code points and only replaces `"` (:1167); patches.py:86/377 same; src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:666 `return str(arg)` stores any length/charset and echoes it byte-perfect; tests/test_nodes.py:58/:322 names are pure ASCII.

**Code depends on it at:** desk.label read-back/resolve (desk.py:1154-1183, resolve by name), diff_states name comparisons, restore_plan `format_token` str (nodes.py:361-364) re-quoting whatever came back.

**Reality:** scales_params.md §4.1/PDF p.25 '12-character max string' on a console whose scribble-strip font is an 8-bit set; HANDOVER §4a confirms the desk truncates at 12. UTF-8 makes é 2 bytes, the typographic apostrophe/quotes an LLM habitually emits (’ “ ”) 3 bytes, emoji 4: an 11-'character' name can be 14+ bytes, the desk truncates mid-sequence and osc.py:228 decodes the read-back with `errors='replace'` → U+FFFD. How the desk renders/stores non-ASCII bytes is not covered by any research doc (implicitly UNCONFIRMED).

**On a real desk:** label('ch.5', name='Tony’s Vox') reports applied='Tony’s Vox'; the strip shows garbage glyphs, reads back as 'Tony�s V…', resolve('tony’s vox') fails, every subsequent diff_snapshot reports the name as changed and restore keeps rewriting it.

**Offline test:** Make FakeDesk store names as the desk does (encode, truncate to 12 BYTES, replace non-printable-ASCII with '?' or drop), then test label()/patch apply with 'Café Größe' and 'Tony’s Vox' → assert the tool either transliterates to ASCII before sending or reports `charset_replaced`, and that read-back == applied. Fails today (fake round-trips Unicode perfectly).

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (low)** — Every citation checks out and there is no fallback the claimant missed. (1) Encoded: src/x32mcp/osc.py:82 `s.encode("utf-8")` with no charset check on string ARGS (addresses ARE forced to printable ASCII at :137/:195 — names are not); desk.py:95 `_NAME_MAX = 12`, :1162-1169 only downgrades `"` and truncates `text[:_NAME_MAX]` by code points; patches.py:86-87/377-383 identical; scales.py:452-455 `str` kind is a bare `str(value)` passthrough; Desk._write_value (desk.py:886-895) sets `applied = spec.to_value(raw)` with no read-after-write, so `applied.name` is whatever was sent; fakedesk.py:666 `return str(arg)` stores any length/any charset and echoes it; fixtures tests/test_nodes.py:58 and :320-324 and tests/integration/test_desk.py:323-354 are pure ASCII. (2) Depends: Desk.resolve (desk.py:543-583) does exact/substring matching on desk-returned names; osc.py:228 decodes read-back with `errors="replace"` — and the module docstring (osc.py:17-18) says this is 'so a stray byte in a desk name can never raise', i.e. the author already anticipated the desk emitting non-UTF-8 name bytes, yet the write path sends multibyte UTF-8 unfiltered. (3) Research: scales_params.md §2 (line 159-160) and §4.1 (line 336) say only 'Max 12 chars … PDF "A 12-character max string"', verified solely against ASCII scene names ("Diazno", "1 Diazno", "USB L", ""); HANDOVER.md §4a line 103-104 'desk truncates names to 12 chars'. No research doc addresses the character set of names at all (grep for utf/ascii/unicode/charset across docs/research hits only OSC address/typetag framing), so 'the desk stores and echoes arbitrary UTF-8, limited by code points not bytes' is an unverified belief that the fake certifies. A '12-character max string' in a C firmware (emulator X32Channel.h `name S32`, XslashSetString) is by any engineering reading a byte buffer; a 12-code-point/14-byte name passes desk.py:1168 untouched. (4) Empirical: in worktree wt/verify-unicode-names (commit 2849b27, tests/integration/test_unicode_names_verify.py) test 1 PASSES today — label('ch.5', name='Sängerin Zoë’') sends 'Sängerin Zoë' (12 cp, 14 B), FakeDesk stores it byte-perfect, resolve('zoë') → ch.5 — and test 2 FAILS today — label('ch.6', name='Tony’s Vox') returns {'applied': {'name': 'Tony’s Vox'}} with no ascii-fold and no charset flag. Caveat: the claimant's specific narrative for 'Tony’s Vox' (reads back as 'Tony�s V…') is over-specific — that name is exactly 12 bytes so byte-truncation alone would not split it; garbling there requires the desk to reject/replace the 3-byte U+2019 sequence, which is plausible (8-bit scribble-strip font, ASCII-only on-desk keyboard) but unverified. The general finding — code-point truncation vs a byte buffer, unfiltered non-ASCII from LLM/CSV patch sheets, fake round-trips it perfectly so label/resolve/diff/restore tests certify it — stands. Severity low is right: names only, no audio path, worst case is a lying `applied`, a failed resolve-by-name and diff/restore churn on that strip.

> **Verifier 2: CONFIRMED (low)** — The encoded belief is real and unverified: osc.py `_pack_string` (src/x32mcp/osc.py:79-82) sends names as UTF-8, desk.label (src/x32mcp/desk.py:1154-1183) and patches.py (:86, :372-378) count the 12-char limit in code points and sanitise only `"`, and FakeDesk `_coerce` for strings is `return str(arg)` (src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:666) — any length, any charset, echoed back byte-perfect; osc.py:228 decodes read-backs with errors='replace'. No research doc says what a real X32 does with non-ASCII bytes: scales_params.md §4.1 / transport.md §6.3 only establish '12-character max string' (an 8-bit C buffer on the desk), and transport.md §9 item list even keeps '>12-char name truncation' UNCONFIRMED (HANDOVER §4a later confirmed truncation at 12 with an ASCII name). So the fake certifies a Unicode round-trip the desk was never shown to honour, and the code has no ASCII transliteration/`charset_replaced` fallback — a genuine member of the class under review.

Skeptical calibration of consequence: nothing here produces a wrong audio write, a safety issue, or garbage into CFS. label() does no read-after-write verify (desk.py:886-895 `_write_value` just writes), so no spurious VALIDATION error. Realistic gig impact: (a) a name like 'José Vox' (≤12 bytes) is stored verbatim and reads back intact — only the scribble strip renders odd glyphs (cosmetic); (b) only a name that is ≤12 code points but >12 bytes (e.g. 'Café Größe' = 10 chars/13 bytes) would, if the desk truncates by bytes, come back with U+FFFD, making resolve-by-that-exact-name fail and diff_snapshot/restore report a perpetual name diff (harmless rewrite). Note the finder's headline example is slightly off: 'Tony’s Vox' is exactly 12 UTF-8 bytes, so it would not be cut mid-sequence under a 12-byte buffer; the 'Café Größe' example does exhibit the claimed failure. LLM tool-call arguments are usually straight-ASCII quotes, so the curly-apostrophe path is plausible but not frequent; accented performer names in Europe are the more likely trigger. Overall: confirmed assumption, cosmetic/minor state-reporting impact, correctly rated low. Offline test as proposed (FakeDesk stores encode→truncate-to-12-bytes→non-printable-ASCII replaced, then assert label()/patch apply either transliterates or flags and read-back == applied) would fail today.

## E93. [low] (transport-connection, partial) A reply always arrives within the per-attempt timeout, so 'the oldest pending waiter for this address' is always the request the reply belongs to. OSC has no request ids; when reply latency exceeds timeout_s the reply to attempt 1 satisfies attempt 2, and the reply to attempt 2 stays in flight to satisfy the NEXT request for that address — which may be a read issued after a write.

**Encoded at:** tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:581-589 (latency test uses 120 ms < 250 ms timeout — never crosses the retry boundary); tests/test_connection.py:245-251,271-274 (retries only ever exercised with dropped, never delayed, replies; FIFO test uses two identical GETs); tests/integration/conftest.py:22 and connection defaults timeout_s=0.5.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:747-769 (_request_bytes: new future per attempt, old one discarded, re-send), :782-795 (_pop_waiter FIFO by key), :139-143 (_reply_key = address only); every Desk._leaf/_read_sections read-after-write; src/x32mcp/desk.py:997-1009 (adjust_level computes base from such a read); cfs.py:1325-1350 (_restore_master read-back).

**Reality:** transport.md §5.4: real-desk latency is UNCONFIRMED ('implies typical replies well under 10 ms on wired LAN'); §2/§10: Wi-Fi bursts queue and drop; nothing bounds reply latency below 500 ms on a congested venue network or while X32-Edit is doing its full sync. The protocol offers no correlation id (§1, §5.1: reply = same address + value), so correctness depends entirely on latency < timeout.

**On a real desk:** Over slow Wi-Fi: get_channel after set_fader shows the pre-write level although the desk applied it (distinct from the known settle race — here the DESK is right and the CLIENT mis-pairs); Desk caches it for 2 s; an adjust_fader/adjust_send then computes from the stale base and writes a jump; CFS _restore_master's read-back never confirms. Probe: latency 300 ms, timeout 250 ms → GET after SET returned the old value while fakedesk.state already held the new one.

**Offline test:** Worktree test test_retry_aliasing_read_after_write_returns_presend_value (/-fake/latency 300 with CONN_OPTS timeout 0.25): FAILS today. Fix direction: after a retried request resolves, quarantine that key for one timeout (drop replies arriving with no waiter AND drop the first reply if a retry happened and a second reply follows), or adapt timeout_s to measured RTT so retries are rare, or for reads prefer /node with a per-request unique path spelling (not available) — at minimum never resolve a waiter created after time T with a datagram that answers a request sent before T (track send time per key and discard replies older than the newest outstanding send when a retry occurred).

> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (medium)** — Core mechanism CONFIRMED and reproduced; impact narrative partly overstated and the trigger is far outside any observed real-desk behaviour, hence PARTIAL.

What checks out:
- connection.py:139-143 `_reply_key` keys a reply by address only (or `node:/path` for /node); :782-795 `_pop_waiter` pops the oldest not-done future for that key; :747-769 `_request_bytes` creates a fresh future per attempt, discards the timed-out one and re-sends. Nothing correlates a datagram with the attempt/request that produced it, nothing quarantines a key after a retry, nothing drains a duplicate reply. An orphan late reply falls through :823-833 and is treated as a pushed update (connection `_cache` written with its value, 'update' published) — so it is either consumed by the NEXT waiter on that key or written into the read-through cache.
- Tests cited are exactly as described: tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:581-589 uses /-fake/latency 120 ms against CONN_OPTS timeout_s=0.25 (tests/integration/conftest.py:22) so a reply never crosses a retry boundary; tests/test_connection.py:245-251 exercises retries only with dropped replies; :271-274 FIFO test uses two identical GETs (aliasing invisible). Production default timeout_s=0.5, retries=2 (connection.py:245-246).
- I ran the claimant's worktree probe (worktrees/assumptions-transport-connection tests/integration/test_transport_assumptions.py::test_retry_aliasing_read_after_write_returns_presend_value, latency 300 ms vs 250 ms timeout): it FAILS on HEAD a408a2a exactly as claimed — GET after SET returns 0.7497 (pre-write) while fakedesk.get() already holds 0.25. desk.py:997-1009 adjust_level does compute base from such a read (via _leaf→_read_sections→node_many, same key scheme `node:/…`), so under the precondition an adjust_fader/adjust_send writes base_stale+delta — a jump, unmitigated by policy (check_relative bounds only delta).
- transport.md §5.4 does say real-desk latency is UNCONFIRMED and 'implies typical replies well under 10 ms on wired LAN', and §1/§5.1 confirm reply = same address + value with no correlation id.

What does not check out / overstated:
- 'CFS _restore_master's read-back never confirms' is wrong: in cfs.py:1325-1350 every GET follows a restore write, so an aliased reply from an earlier iteration still carries the post-write value and confirms (correctly). With latency > 1 s the wait_for(1.0) cancels, but the orphan reply then satisfies the next iteration's GET with a correct value. Restore is not broken by this.
- '§2/§10: Wi-Fi bursts queue and drop' — §2 and §10 document silent datagram LOSS on 54 Mb/s Wi-Fi bursts, not queueing/latency; the >500 ms sustained-RTT precondition is the claimant's engineering argument, not a research citation. The research's own recommendation is a 50–100 ms timeout (i.e. it believes latency is tiny) and the shipped 500 ms default is 5–10x more conservative; HANDOVER §4a records real-desk round trips of a few ms ('restore wrote 3 sections in 9 ms' = three echoed `/` writes; panic 24 msgs in 0.4 ms). A transient stall (roam/power-save) delivers the duplicate replies clumped, which mostly lands the orphan in the no-waiter path (cache write) rather than aliasing a later request; only SUSTAINED RTT above the per-attempt timeout produces the read-after-write mis-pairing.

Net: a genuine untested network assumption (reply latency < per-attempt timeout ⇒ FIFO-by-address pairing is sound) with no fallback in code, correctly located; consequence when triggered includes wrong state reported and a wrong relative write; but the trigger is ~50–150x beyond observed/implied real latency and one of the three cited impact sites (_restore_master) is not actually affected. Medium is defensible on consequence class; likelihood is low on wired LAN, plausible only on badly congested venue Wi-Fi.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — Mechanism is real and reproduced; real-world trigger is not a gig condition, so severity drops to low.

CONFIRMED part: connection.py:747-769 creates a fresh future per attempt and discards the old one; _pop_waiter (782-795) hands any reply for key K to the oldest live waiter; _reply_key (139-143) is address-only. So if the reply to attempt 1 arrives after the per-attempt timeout it resolves attempt 2's future, and the reply to attempt 2 stays in flight and resolves the NEXT waiter on the same key. The finder's worktree test (worktrees/assumptions-transport-connection/tests/integration/test_transport_assumptions.py:26-36, /-fake/latency 300 with CONN_OPTS timeout_s=0.25) fails today exactly as claimed: GET after SET returns 0.7498 while fakedesk already holds 0.25. No existing test crosses the retry boundary with a *delayed* (rather than dropped) reply (test_fakedesk.py:581-589 uses 120 ms < 250 ms; test_connection.py:245-251 drops; :271-274 FIFO with identical GETs). FakeDesk is already capable of the behaviour (fakedesk.py:772-779 latency_ms), so this is a test-coverage assumption, not a fake-fidelity gap.

Why it would not bite at a gig (downgrade): (1) The production default is timeout_s=0.5 (connection.py:245; server.py:154 passes no override), not the fixture's 0.25 the probe used, so every individual reply must take >500 ms. HANDOVER §4a measured the real desk answering a 2101-section /node sweep in 0.28 s on wired LAN (sub-ms per reply, matching transport.md §5.4's 'well under 10 ms'); normal Wi-Fi is 2-20 ms — 25x to 1000x headroom. (2) Transient stalls (Wi-Fi retransmit burst, desk busy during scene load, X32-Edit sync) do NOT create the hazard: after a stall both replies arrive back-to-back, R1 resolves the retry, R2 finds no waiter and is dropped (node key, connection.py:828) or cached as a push (param key, :831-834) which via Desk._on_push (desk.py:282-284) actually invalidates Desk's cache correctly. Only *sustained* RTT in the 500-1000 ms band, with a same-key read-after-write inside that window, mis-pairs — a network nobody can mix on (meters 10+ frames behind, X32-Edit/Mixing Station equally broken; every X32 OSC client shares the no-correlation-id limitation). (3) Client event-loop stalls don't trigger it either: asyncio delivers ready I/O callbacks before due timers in the same iteration, so a buffered reply beats the wait_for timeout. (4) The 'Desk caches it for 2 s' consequence holds only for node-keyed reads; param-keyed orphans self-heal within one latency period.

Residual value: it is silent when it does happen (rtt_ms reports L-T, status looks healthy) and an adjust_fader could compute from a stale base, so a cheap hardening is worthwhile — e.g. count outstanding sends per key and swallow surplus replies after a retry, or keep the original future alive across re-sends and drop one duplicate — plus one FakeDesk test with latency > timeout. But by the brief's rubric this is theoretical / effectively mitigated by the generous default timeout and measured real-desk latency: low, not medium.

## E94. [low] (transport-connection, partial) Link loss is all-or-nothing (cable in / cable out): 1.5 s without an /info answer after 12 s of inbound silence means the desk is gone, so writes must be refused and CFS must abort.

**Encoded at:** tests/test_connection.py:441-467,487-496 and tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:566-579 (silent=True/False only); FakeDesk has drop_next (deterministic count) but no loss rate; HANDOVER §4a validated DEGRADED with a cable pull on wired Ethernet only ('DEGRADED 14 s after the cable came out').

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:245-249 (timeout_s 0.5, retries 2, watchdog_s 12), :909-935 (one failed 3-attempt probe → _degrade), :739-745 (every set()/slash() refused while DEGRADED), :511-512 (reads get a single attempt while DEGRADED — on a lossy link exactly when retries matter most), :937-954 (recovery needs a single-attempt probe to succeed after a 1,2,4,8 s backoff); src/x32mcp/cfs.py:45-48,522,1297-1320 (connection.state=degraded → emergency master restore + ABORT of the ring-out).

**Reality:** transport.md §2 (DOC 269-274): Wi-Fi 'loses datagrams silently'; §5.4 recommends 50-100 ms per request 'with one retry' for LAN latency, but says nothing about declaring the desk dead. Venue 2.4 GHz with a full room routinely shows 10-30 % loss in bursts of seconds. At 20 % one-way loss an idle connection (no meters → 12 s silence is normal → probe every 12 s) has ≈5 % chance per probe cycle of all 3 round trips failing → DEGRADED roughly every 4 min, ≥1 s each.

**On a real desk:** Mid-show on Wi-Fi: 'mute ch 5' → NOT_CONNECTED 'desk not responding' although X32-Edit next to it works; a ring_out in progress ABORTS and fires raw master-restore writes because of a 1.5 s blip; panic degrades to 'unconfirmed'. connection_status flaps degraded/connected in the log.

**Offline test:** Add FakeDesk.loss_rate (seeded RNG, applied inbound and outbound) and run an idle connection with production timeouts for simulated minutes (or scale all timers down): assert state never leaves CONNECTED at 20 % loss and that a write issued during a 1 s burst of 100 % loss is retried/queued rather than refused. Today it degrades. Fix direction: require 2-3 consecutive failed probe cycles (or > N s with zero rx while probes are outstanding) before DEGRADED; keep retries for reads while DEGRADED; let Tier-1 mutes through as send_raw+verify instead of refusing.

> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (low)** — Citations check out, consequences are overstated.

VERIFIED AS CLAIMED: connection.py:245-249 defaults (timeout_s 0.5, retries 2, watchdog_s 12); :511-512 single attempt while DEGRADED; :739-745 _require_writable refuses set()/slash() while DEGRADED; :909-935 one failed 3-attempt /info probe after watchdog_s silence -> _degrade; :937-954 backoff 1,2,4,8 s single-attempt probes; cfs.py:45-48/522/1297-1320 connection.state=degraded -> _lose_connection -> raw master restore + ABORT. FakeDesk (fakedesk.py:57-62,311-312,451,761-793) has only silent (all-or-nothing), drop_next (deterministic reply count) and latency_ms — no loss rate; tests test_connection.py:441-467 and test_fakedesk.py:566-579 use silent True/False only; HANDOVER.md:118-120 validated DEGRADED by cable pull only. transport.md §2 (line 150) does say Wi-Fi 'loses datagrams silently' (though the DOC context is burst /node|/showdump receive overrun, not ambient RF loss) and §5.4 (line 360) recommends 50-100 ms 'with one retry' and says nothing about declaring the desk dead. README.md:808-811 even documents a Wi-Fi Termux tablet host and promises 'expect the desk's watchdog/DEGRADED handling to cover Wi-Fi hiccups' — an untested promise. So the kernel (partial/bursty loss is never modelled; DEGRADED semantics were certified only against total loss) is real.

OVERSTATED / MISSED FALLBACKS: (1) 'ring_out ABORTS because of a 1.5 s blip' is wrong: during a ring-out/watch the CFS's own LiveMeters stream (cfs.py:508,923; meters.py:437-440 renew every 5 s, 20 blobs/s) refreshes _last_rx on every blob (connection.py:815, before blob dispatch), so the watchdog never even probes unless there are >=12 s of ZERO inbound datagrams; abort needs a >=13.5 s total outage (12 s + 1.5 s probe), at which point restoring the master during a feedback-provoking gain raise is the intended safety behaviour, not a spurious abort. At 20 % random loss that requires ~4 consecutive lost renews AND 3 lost probes (~1e-4 per cycle). (2) Recovery does not need the backoff probe: any decodable datagram lifts DEGRADED (connection.py:816-817, and tests/test_connection.py:487-496 which the claimant cites actually proves this). (3) 'mute ch 5 -> NOT_CONNECTED' is largely self-healing: Desk.set_mute (desk.py:1015-1024) reads the leaf first via _leaf->_section->conn.node->request (allowed while DEGRADED); if the desk answers that read the state flips to CONNECTED before conn.set runs; NOT_CONNECTED only surfaces if the section was cached within the 2 s TTL, otherwise the failure mode is a single-attempt read TIMEOUT (36 % vs 4.7 % at 20 % loss) — a real but small effect. (4) panic already falls back to send_raw while DEGRADED (desk.py:1199-1206), as the claimant concedes. (5) At loss rates high enough to flap every few minutes (>=~15-20 % sustained), fire-and-forget conn.set (desk.py:879, no read-back) is already silently losing 1 write in 5 — the DEGRADED refusal is not the operative failure; at realistic unicast Wi-Fi loss (<5 %, MAC-layer retries) an idle link flaps roughly once per several hours for ~1-3 s. Primary documented deployment is a wired Windows PC (README.md:289).

Net: valid untested-assumption finding (no lossy-link model in FakeDesk/responder; README's Wi-Fi claim uncertified), but the gig-failure narrative and the CFS-abort claim do not hold given the meter stream, any-datagram recovery and read-before-write. Downgraded to low.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The mechanism is real and untested, but the gig-level consequences claimed are mostly refuted or already mitigated, and the loss figure that makes it bite is uncited and extreme.

What holds up:
- Test/fixture gap is real: tests/test_connection.py:441-496 and tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py only toggle silent=True/False; FakeDesk (fakedesk.py:57-58, 451, 761-793) offers deterministic drop_next and silent, no probabilistic or burst loss. HANDOVER §4a (lines 118-121) validated DEGRADED only by a wired cable pull. README:811 asserts, untested, that 'the desk's watchdog/DEGRADED handling [will] cover Wi-Fi hiccups' for the Termux tablet host.
- The detector is: 12 s inbound silence (connection.py:909-921) then one /info probe of 3 attempts x 0.5 s (:923, defaults :245-248); all three lost -> _degrade (:934). Recovery: any inbound datagram (:806-807) or a single-attempt probe after 1,2,4,8 s backoff (:937-954). While DEGRADED set()/slash() are refused (:739-745) and request() drops to one attempt (:509-511) — a genuine wart: retries vanish exactly when the link is flaky.
- My Monte Carlo of an idle link with the production timers reproduces the finding's number: 20 % one-way random loss -> ~13 DEGRADED events/h (one per ~4.5 min), mean 3.2 s, 1.2 % duty cycle. But at 10 % it is one per 28 min (1.8 s, 0.11 %), at 5 % one per 3.5 h (1 s), at <=2 % essentially never. Exponential backoff also adds a post-outage write-refusal tail of 1-8.5 s after a multi-second burst (HANDOVER's own 16.7 s recovery 'after 4 probes' is this tail).

What does not hold up:
- 'ring_out ABORTS on a 1.5 s blip': refuted. LiveMeters (meters.py:367-454, cfs.py:508) delivers /meters/15 blobs at ~20 fps through the same socket's on_blob, and every blob refreshes _last_rx (connection.py:803-805); renewals go via send_raw, which is allowed while DEGRADED (:574-577). The watchdog cannot even probe until 12 s pass with zero inbound datagrams, so a CFS abort (cfs.py:1297-1320) needs a >=13.5 s total blackout (or 4 consecutive lost 5-s renewals AND 3 lost probes, ~1e-4). Aborting a ring-out that is raising master gain with no RTA visibility for 13 s is the correct safe behaviour, not a spurious one.
- 'panic degrades to unconfirmed': already mitigated — desk.py:1199-1207 falls back to send_raw, all 24 mutes still go on the wire; only the label changes, and 'unconfirmed' is accurate.
- 'mute ch 5 -> NOT_CONNECTED although X32-Edit works': set_mute (desk.py:1015-1023), set_main_*, set_level etc. read-before-write via _leaf -> node_many; while DEGRADED that read gets one attempt and a successful reply recovers the state before the write (connection.py:806-807), so the tool self-heals with probability (1-p)^2; when it fails it surfaces as an honest unreachable/TIMEOUT. Only write-only paths (mid-ramp steps, raw conn.set) hit the refusal.
- The '10-30 % venue Wi-Fi loss' premise is not from docs/research: transport.md §2 (line 149) documents silent loss only for bulk /node and /showdump bursts over 54 Mb/s Wi-Fi (receive overrun), and §5.4 (line 358) recommends 50-100 ms with one retry — the code is far more tolerant (500 ms x 3). Unicast UDP over 802.11 gets MAC-layer retransmission; sustained 20 % application-layer loss means the link is at the edge of usability, and on such a link 20 % of the product's un-acked fire-and-forget writes (conn.set, transport.md §5.2; Desk._write does no read-back, desk.py:871-884) vanish silently while CONNECTED — a far worse defect than a 1 % honest-refusal duty cycle. Realistic Wi-Fi failure is bursty, and for sub-1.5 s bursts the 3-attempt probe already rides through.
- Primary deployment is a wired Windows PC on the desk's LAN (README:289); the Wi-Fi OSC link exists only in the optional Termux tablet-host scenario (README:795-811).

Net: a legitimate untested assumption (no partial/burst-loss fixture; reads lose retries while DEGRADED; backoff tail after bursts) that on a Wi-Fi-hosted idle link can produce an occasional spurious, retryable NOT_CONNECTED for a write-only call issued seconds after a dropout. No wrong write, no safety impact, CFS consequence refuted, panic mitigated, most tools self-heal. Downgraded from medium to low. The proposed offline test (FakeDesk.loss_rate / burst schedule with seeded RNG, scaled timers, assert no DEGRADED at realistic loss and bounded post-burst recovery) is still worth adding, mainly to pin the README:811 claim and to justify keeping read retries while DEGRADED and capping the backoff tail.

## E95. [low] (transport-connection, confirmed) Sending /xremote every 8 s means we are registered for pushes: heartbeat_ok is set when the datagram is SENT, and the desk is assumed to always have a free client slot and to have received every renewal.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:845-853 (the 5th client only produces a log.warning inside the fake — invisible to the client, and no test registers five clients); tests/test_connection.py:197-199 (heartbeat_ok asserted from '/xremote was received ≥3 times' on a lossless link); tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:219-261 (two clients only).

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:891-899 (_heartbeat_ok = True on send), :451-464 (status.heartbeat_ok), :247 heartbeat_s=8.0 vs the 10 s lease (one lost renewal = up to 6 s unregistered, during which another app can take the slot); src/x32mcp/desk.py:232,282-283 (node-cache coherence with front-panel/X32-Edit moves relies on pushes; otherwise stale for read_cache_ttl_s=2 s, device.yaml:739) → :997-1009 adjust_level base; dashboard 'update' feed (connection.py:833-834).

**Reality:** transport.md §2/§4.1: 'maximum four active clients' (DOC 446-455, X32.c MAX_CLIENTS 4); '/xremote itself is never acked' (§4.1); emulator function_xremote returns 0 silently when the table is full (X32.c 3108-3136 'no room for new clients! (todo; another return status?)'). A gig commonly has X32-Edit on the FOH laptop + Mixing Station/X32-Q on 2-3 phones/iPads for IEM mixes = 4 slots gone before we connect.

**On a real desk:** As 5th client we never receive a push: connection_status says heartbeat_ok=true; the dashboard never shows operator moves; get_* lag the desk by up to 2 s; an adjust_send +3 dB issued right after the monitor engineer pulled that send down on his iPad computes from the old level and puts it back up (+3). Probe: 4 other clients registered → our port absent from fakedesk.clients, zero pushes, heartbeat_ok True.

**Offline test:** Worktree test test_fifth_xremote_client_gets_no_pushes_and_status_should_say_so FAILS today. Make it detectable: count pushes ('pushes_seen', 'last_push_age_s') in ConnectionStatus and drop heartbeat_ok's claim; optionally self-test registration once after connect by SETting a harmless leaf from a second ephemeral socket and expecting the echo on the main one (§4.2: pushes go to every OTHER client); renew every ~3 s so a single lost /xremote cannot lapse the lease.

(todo; another return status?)'; §9 item 7 'no acks for SET//xremote//renew; silence = ignored or lost'.
