## E96. [low] (transport-connection, confirmed) Discovery: the host's own name resolves (via getaddrinfo(gethostname())) to its LAN IPv4 address(es), every LAN is a /24 so '<a.b.c>.255' is the directed broadcast, and the desk answers the limited broadcast 255.255.255.255 as a fallback.

**Encoded at:** tests/conftest.py:75-90 (_is_broadcast: ANY address ending in .255 or 255.255.255.255 is delivered to every in-memory endpoint — broadcast cannot fail in the sandbox); tests/test_connection.py:564-574 and tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:48-51 (discovery verified only via the 127.0.0.1 unicast target); src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:832-834 answers /xinfo from anywhere.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:714-729 (_discovery_targets: hosts from getaddrinfo(gethostname()); ip.rsplit('.',1)[0]+'.255'; silently falls back to ['255.255.255.255','127.0.0.1'] on gaierror/timeout), :654-712 (discover); server discover_consoles tool (server.py:625-641). Measured on this Mac: getaddrinfo(gethostname()) → gaierror(8) and _discovery_targets(10023) == [('255.255.255.255',10023), ('127.0.0.1',10023)] — the CONFIRMED mechanism is never used.

**Reality:** transport.md §3.2: CONFIRMED only for the SUBNET-DIRECTED broadcast derived from the interface address (X32_Command sets the last octet of its own IP to 0xff, SO_BROADCAST, 5 tries × 500 ms); 'Whether 255.255.255.255 limited broadcast also works: UNCONFIRMED'. macOS/Termux commonly cannot resolve their own hostname; limited broadcast leaves only via the default-route interface (at a gig: Wi-Fi for internet, while the desk hangs off a USB-Ethernet dongle); venue networks are often /16 or 10.x.

**On a real desk:** discover_consoles returns 'found 0 console(s)' at the venue although the desk is up and X32-Edit sees it; the operator has to read the IP off the desk's Setup screen. Code depends on an UNCONFIRMED item with no working fallback on the commonest laptop OS.

**Offline test:** Unit-test _discovery_targets with loop.getaddrinfo monkeypatched to raise gaierror / return only 127.0.1.1 and assert at least one per-interface directed broadcast is still produced (enumerate interfaces without DNS: a UDP socket connect() to 10.255.255.255/the configured X32_HOST to learn the egress IP, socket.if_nameindex()+ioctl on POSIX, or send /xinfo on every interface's broadcast obtained from `ip`/`ifconfig` parsing) and that non-/24 masks are honoured; make the shim deliver '.255' only to endpoints in the same emulated subnet so the test can fail.

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (medium)** — Both citations check out and no fallback was missed. docs/research/transport.md §3.2 (line 213) says verbatim that broadcast discovery is CONFIRMED only for the subnet-directed broadcast X32_Command derives from its own interface IP (last octet -> 0xff, SO_BROADCAST, 5x500 ms) and '(Whether 255.255.255.255 limited broadcast also works: UNCONFIRMED; Maillot uses the subnet-directed broadcast.)'; HANDOVER §8 (l.256-257) and README l.897 repeat that limited-broadcast /xinfo is an open real-desk unknown. src/x32mcp/connection.py:714-729 (_discovery_targets) builds targets as ['255.255.255.255','127.0.0.1', self._host if set] plus ip.rsplit('.',1)[0]+'.255' for each non-127.x address returned by loop.getaddrinfo(socket.gethostname()) within 1 s, and silently swallows OSError/TimeoutError — there is no interface enumeration, no netmask handling, no use of the configured/egress interface. So the only CONFIRMED mechanism is reachable solely through hostname self-resolution, which fails on macOS when the hostname is not DNS/mDNS-resolvable (reproduced here: getaddrinfo('jimb-KFCWT2NV9R') -> gaierror(8), leaving exactly [255.255.255.255, 127.0.0.1]; caveat: the Seatbelt sandbox may itself block mDNSResponder, but the failure mode is a well-known macOS one) and on stock Debian/Ubuntu where /etc/hosts maps the hostname to 127.0.1.1 (filtered by startswith('127.')). In those cases discover() (654-712) depends entirely on the UNCONFIRMED limited broadcast, which additionally egresses only via the default-route interface (Wi-Fi, not the dongle the desk is on). The /24 assumption mirrors X32_Command so it is 'as confirmed', but a /16 or 10.x venue LAN makes a.b.c.255 a dead unicast — a fair networking-common-sense point, weaker than the main one. Tests: tests/test_connection.py:564-574 and tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:48-51 assert only on the 127.0.0.1 unicast hit; nothing in tests/ exercises _discovery_targets, getaddrinfo failure, or the broadcast path (grep confirms). fakedesk.py:832-834 answers /xinfo to any sender. One citation nuance: tests/conftest.py:75-90 (_is_broadcast delivering any *.255 to every endpoint) is accurate as to content but that file is the sandbox-only socket shim (git-excluded via .git/info/exclude), not a repo fixture — the in-repo point stands without it. Real-desk session (HANDOVER l.89,138) used connect('192.168.1.139') directly from a Windows PC on a /24, so discovery was never validated on hardware. Impact: discover_consoles (server.py:625-641) returns 'No console answered /xinfo ... (is the desk on the same LAN and UDP 10023 open?)' while X32-Edit sees the desk — a T0 tool failing spuriously/misleadingly at a gig; workaround is typing the IP into connect(), so no wrong write. Medium per the rubric (borderline low given connect(host) works and docs flag the 255.255.255.255 unknown, but the hostname-resolution dependence of the CONFIRMED path is undocumented and untested).

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The substance is real but the gig consequence is overstated. TRUE: (1) src/x32mcp/connection.py:714-729 builds targets as ['255.255.255.255','127.0.0.1', <connected host>] plus '<a.b.c>.255' for each non-127 IPv4 from getaddrinfo(gethostname()), silently swallowing gaierror/timeout; the first target is the item transport.md §3.2 marks UNCONFIRMED and the '.255' suffix hard-codes /24 (on this Mac's en0, 10.138.48.131/21, it would emit 10.138.48.255, a unicast address, not the subnet broadcast 10.138.55.255). (2) No test exercises _discovery_targets at all (grep: zero hits in tests/); both discovery tests (tests/test_connection.py:564-574, tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:48-51) pass purely because '127.0.0.1' is in the hard-coded list and the fake is bound to loopback, a path that does not exist at a venue; the directed-broadcast branch is never even produced under test (the shim maps gethostname()→127.0.0.1, which the code filters). (3) Discovery was never run against the real desk: HANDOVER §4a drove M5 with connect('192.168.1.139') directly, and §8 / README:897 still list limited-broadcast /xinfo as an open UNCONFIRMED. (4) I reproduced getaddrinfo(gethostname()) → gaierror(8) and _discovery_targets(10023) == [('255.255.255.255',10023),('127.0.0.1',10023)] here. OVERSTATED: (a) the gaierror measurement was taken inside a sandbox that blocks networking (mDNSResponder), so it does not prove macOS-in-general; more importantly the documented deployment (README:289, HANDOVER §4a: Windows PC 192.168.1.231, desk 192.168.1.139) is Windows on a /24, where getaddrinfo(own computer name) returns the adapter IPs without DNS, so the CONFIRMED X32_Command mechanism (192.168.1.255) IS produced at Jim's gig. (b) The /24 assumption is exactly what the CONFIRMED reference implementation does (X32_Command sets last octet 0xff); research offers no better ground truth, so the fake is not contradicting verified desk behaviour. (c) The desk answering 255.255.255.255 is UNCONFIRMED but physically near-certain for any wildcard-bound UDP stack; the genuine risk is sender-side egress interface selection (Wi-Fi default route vs Ethernet dongle), a host-OS issue, not a desk belief. (d) tests/conftest.py cited as 'encoded_at' is the untracked review-sandbox shim, not a product fixture. (e) Consequence is benign: a Tier-0 convenience tool returns 0 consoles with a mildly misleading hint (server.py:639); no write, no safety path, CFS never consumes it; the documented primary path is X32_HOST / connect(host) (README:370, :439) and the IP is on the desk's Setup screen. That is an inconvenience, not 'tool reports wrong desk state'. Net: a valid untested-assumption finding (discovery certified only via loopback unicast; primary target UNCONFIRMED; /24 + hostname-resolution assumptions) worth a unit test of _discovery_targets and a real-desk check, but severity low, not medium.

## E97. [low] (transport-connection, confirmed) Every command is idempotent, so request() may re-send anything on a missing reply; and the desk answers /save as fast as a parameter GET.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:1159-1184 (_h_save replies ',si scene 1' in the same event-loop tick; /load /delete /rename likewise :1186-1238); tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:474-490 and test_desk/test_server scene tests run at zero latency; connection.py docstring :22-23 justifies retries for slash() ('idempotent') but request() applies them to everything.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:495-514 (request(): retries default 2 for any address); src/x32mcp/desk.py:1291-1310 (save_scene → conn.request('/save','scene',idx,name,notes) with default retries → up to 3 /save datagrams; RequestTimeout → DeskError TIMEOUT although the scene may have been written 1-3 times).

**Reality:** fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4 (DOC fn.39-41): 'The load/save/copy operation is not necessarily fully completed when the status is returned' — the status timing of a flash write is unspecified and real-desk latency is UNCONFIRMED (transport.md §5.4); transport.md §5.3: silence is the only error signal, so a slow status is indistinguishable from a lost one. /save, /load, /copy, /delete, /-action/* are side-effecting, not idempotent reads.

**On a real desk:** save_scene over Wi-Fi or on a busy desk: the scene is saved twice or three times (extra flash writes, scene list flickers on X32-Edit) and, if all statuses are >0.5 s late, the tool reports TIMEOUT 'no reply to /save' for a save that happened — the operator saves again into another slot or distrusts the tool. Probe: latency 300 ms → '/save reached the desk 2 times' with a success reply.

**Offline test:** Worktree test test_save_is_sent_once_even_when_the_status_reply_is_slow FAILS today. Fix: request(..., retries=0, timeout=~3 s) for /save,/load,/copy,/delete,/rename,/add and any /-action that is answered; on timeout read /-show/showfile/scene/NNN back (name/hasdata) before declaring failure.

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (medium)** — All citations check out. connection.py:495-514 request() applies the constructor default retries (connection.py:245-246: timeout_s=0.5, retries=2 → 3 sends, and server.py:154 instantiates X32Connection with empty conn_opts so production uses those defaults) to any address; _request_bytes (connection.py:747-769) re-sends the identical datagram on each per-attempt timeout. desk.py:1291-1310 save_scene calls self._conn.request('/save','scene',idx,text,notes) with no retries/timeout override and maps RequestTimeout to DeskError('TIMEOUT', 'no reply to /save') with no read-back of /-show/showfile/scene/NNN. The module docstring (connection.py:22-23) justifies retrying only for slash() as 'idempotent'; nothing distinguishes side-effecting commands. FakeDesk _h_save (fakedesk.py:1159-1184) replies synchronously in the same tick, and /load,/delete,/rename (1186-1238) likewise, so no test ever exercised a status slower than the retry timeout; tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:474-490 runs the scene round-trip at zero latency. Research citations are accurate: fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4 line 564 quotes DOC fn.39-41 'The load/save/copy operation is not necessarily fully completed when the status is returned'; transport.md §5.4 line 358 'UNCONFIRMED numeric latency of a real desk'; §5.3 line 348 silence is the only error signal. I ran the claimant's worktree test (worktrees/assumptions-transport-connection, tests/integration/test_transport_assumptions.py:73-80) and it fails today: with /-fake/latency 300 (fixture timeout_s=0.25, retries=1) '/save reached the desk 2 times' while the caller still gets ('scene',1) — the late first reply satisfies the second attempt's future. Same mechanism at production 0.5 s with a >0.5 s or lost status datagram (Wi-Fi). No fallback exists (no retries=0 for /save, no post-timeout read-back). Caveat: the DOC footnote implies the status is returned early (before completion), so a slow status is speculative; but a lost reply datagram triggers the identical duplicate-save path, and an all-attempts loss yields a false TIMEOUT for a save that happened. Duplicate save to the same slot/name is mostly benign (extra flash write, near-identical content), so the real harm is the tool misreporting — fits medium (tool reports wrong state / fails spuriously), not high. Only /save is affected in Desk today (recall uses fire-and-forget /-action/goscene via _write at desk.py:1262; /load,/delete,/rename,/copy are not called by Desk), so the blast radius is narrower than the finding's list, but the core claim stands.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — Mechanism CONFIRMED, consequence and scope OVERSTATED; downgraded to low.

What is true: X32Connection.request() (src/x32mcp/connection.py:495-514, defaults timeout_s=0.5, retries=2 at :245-246, production App passes no overrides server.py:154) re-sends any address on a missed reply, and Desk.save_scene (desk.py:1298) calls conn.request('/save', ...) with those defaults. FakeDesk._h_save (fakedesk.py:1159-1184) replies in the same tick and every scene test runs at zero latency, so the suite never exercised a slow/lost status. The connection docstring's 'idempotent' justification (:22-23) covers slash(), not /save. The slice's worktree test fails today ('/save reached the desk 2 times' at 300 ms latency vs the 250 ms test timeout), and my own probe under PRODUCTION defaults (worktree verify-save-retries-repro, commit 8d73076) shows: 0/400 ms -> 1 datagram ok; 600 ms -> 2 datagrams ok; 1200 ms -> 3 datagrams ok; 1600 ms -> 3 datagrams + DeskError TIMEOUT although scene 9 IS stored.

Why it would rarely bite at a gig, and mildly when it does:
1. Scope: /save is the ONLY side-effecting command routed through request() in product code (grep: desk.py:1298 is the sole call site; recall_scene uses fire-and-forget set + read-back verify; /load,/copy,/delete,/rename,/add are not sent by any tool). The finding's list of affected commands is hypothetical.
2. A duplicated /save carries identical args (same slot, same name, same live state within 0.5 s) — the outcome on the desk is the same scene in the same slot. 'Extra flash writes' and 'scene list flickers in X32-Edit' are cosmetic; no wrong write, no audio consequence, nobody hears anything.
3. The spurious-TIMEOUT half needs the FIRST status to arrive > 1.5 s after the first send (pending waiters are a per-address FIFO, so a late reply to attempt 1 satisfies attempt 2 or 3 — the finding's '>0.5 s late' framing is off by 3x), or all three reply datagrams lost. fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4 (DOC fn.39-41) says the status is returned BEFORE the operation necessarily completes — i.e. the status is prompt, not gated on the flash write; transport.md §5.4 puts typical wired replies well under 10 ms (real-desk figure UNCONFIRMED). save_scene was never run live (HANDOVER §4a 'Still to do', desk in CUES mode), so there is no real-desk evidence of a slow /save status. On a Wi-Fi link bad enough to stall > 1.5 s, every read (1.5 s budget) and the watchdog are already failing; /save is not special.
4. If the spurious TIMEOUT did occur, the message is 'no reply to /save' (ambiguous, not a false 'not saved'), and the operator's natural retry re-saves the same slot harmlessly.

So: a genuine baked-in assumption (retry policy for reads applied to a side-effecting command; fake answers instantly) with a trivial fix (retries=0 + ~2-3 s timeout for /save, read /-show/showfile/scene/NNN hasdata/name back before declaring failure), but the realistic gig impact is cosmetic-to-minor, not 'tool reports wrong state'. Severity low. Related but separate (not credited to this finding): the unmatched duplicate '/save ,si scene 1' reply is filed as a pushed parameter update and cached under '/save' (slice test 5) — also cosmetic.

## E98. [low] (transport-connection, partial) The desk comes back at the same IP address it had when connect() ran; the name/IP is resolved exactly once and the reconnect loop probes that address forever.

**Encoded at:** tests/test_connection.py:469-485 (reconnect after responder restart 'on the same port … same socket, never re-bound'), :498-507 (resolve once is the asserted behaviour); src/x32mcp/connection.py:27-29 docstring makes it a decision.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:375-401 (_resolve once), :937-954 (_reconnect_loop probes self._host only; never re-resolves, never re-runs discover(), never matches by console name), :869-877 (error text 'desk not responding' regardless of cause); server.py autoconnect uses X32_HOST once (:185-190).

**Reality:** HANDOVER §4a: 'the PSU fault reboots the desk, so state may not survive' — a reboot re-runs DHCP; /-prefs/ip/dhcp exists (transport.md §6.5 '-prefs/ip (+/dhcp /addr /mask /gateway)'), so a DHCP-configured desk on a venue router can return with a new lease/IP. transport.md §3.2 gives the tool everything needed to re-find it (/xinfo broadcast reply carries IP + console name).

**On a real desk:** After the brown-out the desk is back and X32-Edit (which re-discovers) reconnects, but x32-mcp sits in DEGRADED 'reconnecting; N probe(s)' indefinitely, refusing every write; connection_status implies the desk is still down. The operator must notice, find the new IP on the desk screen and call connect() by hand mid-show.

**Offline test:** Integration test: connect to FakeDesk A, stop it, start FakeDesk B (same name 'X32-FAKE') on another port/emulated IP, assert the connection recovers to B within a few backoff cycles (reconnect loop falls back to discover() and matches ConsoleInfo.name/model after K failed probes, re-resolving a hostname if one was given). Today it never recovers.

> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (low)** — Code citations check out: connect() resolves the host exactly once (connection.py:301-308, _resolve at :375-401, docstring decision at :27-29), _send() always targets (self._host, self._port) (:733-737), and _reconnect_loop (:937-954) only re-sends /info to that fixed numeric address — it never re-resolves, never calls discover(), never matches by console name. server.py:185-190 autoconnects from X32_HOST once. tests/test_connection.py:469-485 (restart on the same port, 'same socket, never re-bound') and :498-509 (resolve hostname once, _host == '127.0.0.1') encode exactly that. DESIGN.md §8 (:373-375) specifies the reconnect loop as 're-/info until it answers', so this is by design, and the M5 live test (HANDOVER §4a 'Degraded + auto-reconnect … reconnected by itself 16.7 s later') only exercised a cable pull where the IP cannot change.

But the 'reality' leg is the claimant's inference, not what the cited sources say. HANDOVER §4a:133-134 says 'the PSU fault reboots the desk, so state may not survive. Snapshot first, power-cycle, then diff_snapshot' — that is about mixer parameter state, not the network address; the same section records 'desk 192.168.1.139' as a stable 'fact worth keeping' and says nothing about DHCP. transport.md §6.5:515 merely lists -prefs/ip/dhcp as an existing node; §3.2 confirms /xinfo broadcast discovery returns IP+name. Nothing in research/handover says this desk is on DHCP or that an X32 returns from a reboot with a different lease; ordinary DHCP behaviour is to re-issue the same lease to the same MAC, and live-sound practice is static IPs. The X32-Edit 'which re-discovers' claim is also unsourced.

The consequence is also milder than stated: if the desk did move IP, the connection sits in DEGRADED, writes are refused (fail-safe, no wrong write, CFS cannot act), connection_status truthfully reports DEGRADED with host and probe count (server.py:705-727) — 'not answering at that address' is accurate, not a lie — and the existing discover_consoles + connect tools (server.py:626-632, :192-201) recover it without reading the IP off the desk screen. So: a real robustness gap (no re-discovery/re-resolution in the reconnect path, worth the proposed FakeDesk-B-on-new-address test), but premised on an unverified DHCP scenario and with fail-safe, truthfully-reported behaviour and a manual tool path — low, not medium.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The assumption is real and is encoded where the finding says: connect() resolves once (src/x32mcp/connection.py:308, _resolve at :375-401), _send() always targets self._host (:733-737), and _reconnect_loop (:937-954) only re-binds the local socket and re-probes /info at that one numeric address — it never re-resolves a name, never calls discover(), never matches by console name. tests/test_connection.py:469-485 asserts recovery to a responder restarted on the same port and :498-507 asserts resolve-once. So if the desk genuinely returned on a different IP, x32-mcp would sit in DEGRADED forever and connection_status would say 'desk … is not answering (reconnecting; N probe(s))' (server.py:725-726) until someone calls connect() with the new address.

But as a skeptical verifier I cannot rate this above low, for five reasons:
1. It is an explicit, documented design decision (connection.py:27-29 docstring, README 'reconnect loop probes … until the desk answers again'), not a hidden belief the emulator smuggled in — the class REVIEW_BRIEF §2 is after is beliefs nobody knew they held.
2. The project already mitigates it operationally: docs/GIG_CHECKLIST.md:20 (Pre-show, Power and network) requires 'static or reserved IPs for the desk and the PC'. That is standard live-sound practice for a control LAN and removes the scenario entirely.
3. The 'reality' cited does not establish that a real desk changes IP on reboot. HANDOVER §4a only says a PSU fault reboots the desk and 'state may not survive' (desk parameters), and transport.md §6.5 only lists /-prefs/ip/dhcp as an existing node. A DHCP server re-offers the same binding to the same MAC in the normal case (lease still valid; dnsmasq-class routers even allocate deterministically by MAC hash), so an address change after a seconds-long PSU reboot needs a compound failure (lease expiry/pool churn or a router that also lost its lease table). Jim's desk (192.168.1.139, HANDOVER §4a) reconnected by itself after the cable pull; nothing in the research says it would come back elsewhere after the pending power-cycle test.
4. The failure mode is safe and honest, not 'tool lies / wrong write': writes are refused with NOT_CONNECTED, a running ring-out restores master and aborts, reads time out, audio is unaffected, and connection_status reports ok:false/DEGRADED with the probe count. Recovery is available through the conversational path without touching config: discover_consoles (server.py:626-632, conn.discover opens its own broadcast socket and works while DEGRADED) then connect(new_ip). The golden rule in GIG_CHECKLIST already routes mid-set emergencies to the physical desk/X32-Edit anyway.
5. The claim that 'X32-Edit (which re-discovers) reconnects' is unsupported: X32-Edit connects to a chosen IP and, like Maillot's X32_Command (transport.md §3.2: broadcast /xinfo once at startup, then 'talks unicast to that IP'), does not chase a desk to a new address. x32-mcp's behaviour matches the reference clients.

What survives: (a) when X32_HOST is a hostname, re-resolving on each reconnect probe would be cheap and strictly better (the resolve-once rationale is about per-datagram sendto cost, not about reconnect probes seconds apart); (b) after K unanswered probes the DEGRADED message could suggest discover_consoles / name the possibility that the desk moved, instead of 'reconnecting' indefinitely. Both are robustness/UX improvements for an edge case the checklist already tells the operator to prevent — low severity, not medium.

- connection.py:325-339 parses /info model into ConsoleInfo and never branches on it; grep confirms ConsoleInfo.model is only used in log/summary strings (server.py:188,636,661,716; webui.py:507). No code queries /-ha/NN/index either (grep: zero hits in src/ and device.yaml), although scales_params.md §12.3 says 'Prefer querying /-ha/NN/index over computing' and §12.4 (the algorithm desk.py:722-781 implements) is explicitly UNCONFIRMED.
- desk.py:722-781 headamp_index_for: block_base(r) returns r*8 for r in 0..3 (AN1-8..AN25-32) and userrout values 1..32 → 0..31 unconditionally, so local inputs 17-32 resolve to head amps 016-031 on every model; its docstring promises None 'when no preamp sits there'. set_phantom (desk.py:1352-1371) writes /headamp/NNN/phantom for whatever index comes back and returns on:True; discover_mics (provision.py:582) sets physical=(index is not None).
- Reality: transport.md §3.1 line 163 lists X32, X32RACK, X32C, X32P, X32CORE, M32, M32C, M32R. Stronger than the claimant cited: scales_params.md §12.2 (lines 767-771) states VERIFIED-CORRECTED local head-amp counts — full-size 32, Compact/Producer/Rack 16, Core none — and 'All models use the same 000..127 numbering; local indices without hardware are simply unused.' So the research hands the code a per-model table it ignores; the OSC leaves exist regardless, so writes/reads to phantom/gain of non-existent preamps succeed silently. HANDOVER §4b confirms discover_mics reported 7 candidates for 1 real mic (correctly cited, though §4b attributes it to no meter cross-check, not model).
- No fallback found: no model table, no /-ha read-back, no meter-activity cross-check (provision.py has none; §4b lists it as outstanding).

Overstated / not supported:
- 'On the X32 Rack this project targets, with factory routing: set_phantom(ch 20) → head amp 019'. The research does not state per-model factory input routing; on Compact/Producer/Rack the factory default for inputs 17-32 is AES50 A1-16 (general product knowledge), which would resolve ch 20 to head amp 035 (a stage-box preamp that may or may not exist — a different assumption). And the actual target desk (HANDOVER §4a) uses FW-4 user routing (ch1→local 1, ch2-3→card, ch4→AES50-A 1), not AN17-32. The head-amp-019 failure needs a Rack/Compact/Producer carrying a scene with Local 17-32 routing (common when a show file is authored on a full-size X32 or X32-Edit) or any X32 Core/M32C with local routing — realistic but narrower than 'factory routing'.
- 'discover_mics lists ch 17-32 as routed-to-preamp candidates': physical_input would be wrongly True, but a channel is only listed if it also sends ≥ floor to the bus, is in the patch, or is in mute group 6 (provision.py:593-595); include additionally needs unmuted+sending. So it mis-flags rather than unconditionally lists.
- 'a future output/AES50 feature would address XLR outs 9-16' is speculative; no current code depends on the 16-XLR-out count.

Net: the encoded assumption (one physical I/O complement for every model; Rack-labelled fake with 32 live local preamps) and the code's dependence on it are real and untested; the research explicitly contradicts it (§12.2). The concrete gig scenario is plausible but mis-specified. Severity medium per rubric (set_phantom reports phantom ON for a preamp that does not physically exist; discover_mics physical_input wrong) — at the low end: the write is harmless, and the trigger requires a non-full-size model with local-17+ (or, on a Core, any local) routing. Offline test proposal (parametrise FakeDesk by model with a local-preamp count so /headamp/016-031 have no 'hardware' and AN17-32 inputs are silent; assert headamp_index_for('ch.20') is None / set_phantom NOT_SUPPORTED on X32RACK) is sound and would fail today.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The factual core holds: ConsoleInfo.model is parsed (connection.py:94/325-339) and only ever printed (server.py:188,661,716); there is no per-model table; headamp_index_for (desk.py:722-781) maps any local source 1..32 to head amp 000..031 regardless of model; the FakeDesk defaults to model='X32RACK' (fakedesk.py:288) while emulating 32 live local inputs with AN17-32 factory routing (fakedesk.py:136); and docs/research/scales_params.md §12.2 explicitly records the per-model local preamp counts (full-size 32, Compact/Producer/Rack 16, Core 0) — so the information was available and ignored. That is a genuine 'one console model' assumption baked into fake + descriptor.

But argued from the gig consequence, it is weak and largely already covered:
1. Research §12.2 also says 'All models use the same 000..127 numbering; local indices without hardware are simply unused' — i.e. the real Rack's OSC server accepts /headamp/016-031 reads/writes exactly as the FakeDesk does. The fake is not misbehaving at the protocol level; the gap is only that nothing physical sits behind those indices.
2. set_phantom(ch 20) on a Rack with local-17-24 routing: the write is a harmless no-op and the tool returns on:true. The finding's 'condenser stays dead, operator hunts cables' scenario is not physically constructible — a Rack has no XLR jack 17-32 to plug the condenser into. If the mic is on an AES50 stagebox, either routing already points at AES50 (headamp_index_for then resolves 032+ correctly and real 48 V appears) or routing is wrong and the channel carries no audio at all regardless of phantom — the misleading 'on:true' delays a routing diagnosis, nothing more. No wrong voltage is ever applied anywhere. On the actual target desk (X32RACK-Jim) user routing is in force (ch1 local 1, ch2-3 card, ch4 AES50-A1), so the factory-routing premise does not even apply there.
3. discover_mics over-inclusion of ch 17-32: requires those channels to be unmuted AND sending to the monitored bus above the -40 dB floor (provision.py:582-591), an odd state for inputs that cannot carry audio; and it is a strict sub-case of the limitation HANDOVER §4b already records ('cannot tell a connected mic from an empty channel … 7 candidates for 1 mic') whose proposed fix (cross-check meter activity) would eliminate non-existent preamps too, since they read silent. Candidates are surfaced for human confirmation (server.py:132) and only gate preflight blockers/warnings — CFS does not write based on them.
4. The 'future output/AES50 feature would address XLR outs 9-16' point is speculative; no such code exists.
So: real un-modelled assumption, correct file:line citations, but the concrete failure is a misleading success report / extra informational candidates, not a wrong write or safety issue, and the discover_mics half is already a documented known limitation. Downgrade medium -> low.

## E100. [low] (transport-connection, confirmed) Any inbound message with arguments whose address starts with '/' and is not /info,/xinfo,/status,'/' or 'node' is a pushed PARAMETER update — so late or duplicate replies to commands (/save, /load, /delete, /rename, /copy, /add status, '/-action/* ,i 0' acknowledgements, stale GET replies after a retry) are cached as parameter values and published as 'update' events.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:71 (_NOT_PARAMS = {/info,/xinfo,/status,/}) and docstring :34-35; tests/test_connection.py:361-374 only push genuine parameter addresses; FakeDesk never answers /-action/goscene (fakedesk.py:53-55 docstring) so the ack path is never exercised.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:828-834 (_cache[msg.address] = value; on_update callbacks; events.publish('update')); src/x32mcp/desk.py:282-283 (_on_push invalidation), webui/event log consumers.

**Reality:** fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4 (DOC p.70-71): several /-action/* commands 'are replied with a [0], indicating the command has been processed' and the best inference is that /-action/goscene answers '/-action/goscene ,i 0'; /save,/load,/delete,/rename,/copy answer ',si <type> 1|0' (§6.4 table). None of these are parameter values. transport.md §5.4: reply latency unbounded → late GET replies exist.

**On a real desk:** After recall_scene the event log/dashboard shows a parameter 'update /-action/goscene = 0'; after a retried save an 'update /save = (scene,1)'; a stale fader value from a late GET reply is written into the connection cache with a fresh timestamp (harmless today only because nothing calls get_cached). Probe: duplicate /save status was published as an update and cached under '/save'.

**Offline test:** Worktree test test_late_command_reply_is_not_a_parameter_update FAILS today. Fix: treat as parameter push only addresses the descriptor knows (leaf or node path), or extend _NOT_PARAMS to the command family (/save /load /delete /rename /copy /add /-action/* /renew /meters /formatsubscribe /batchsubscribe) and never cache from an unmatched reply of a key that had a retry in the last timeout window.

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (low)** — Both citations hold and the behaviour reproduces on HEAD a408a2a.

Code: src/x32mcp/connection.py:71 defines _NOT_PARAMS = {/info,/xinfo,/status,/}; _handle_datagram (connection.py:820-834) pops a waiter by address, routes blobs, drops only node/_NOT_PARAMS/arg-less/non-slash messages, and otherwise unconditionally does `self._cache[msg.address] = (ts, value)`, calls every on_update callback and publishes an 'update' event (comment at :828 even says "or a late reply"). There is no descriptor check at this layer. Desk.recall_scene (desk.py:1262) sends /-action/goscene through _write → conn.set, which is fire-and-forget (connection.py:520-530) so no waiter ever exists for the desk's acknowledgement; save_scene (desk.py:1298) uses conn.request with the default 2 retries, so a slow status produces a duplicate reply with no waiter.

Research: fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4 table row for /-action/goscene says exactly what is claimed (UNCONFIRMED; best inference from DOC p.70-71 that /-action/* commands are "replied with a [0]" and to "expect /-action/goscene ,i 0 plus the /xremote burst"); /load /save /delete /rename /copy replies are VERIFIED as ',si <type> 1'. transport.md §5.4 marks real-desk latency UNCONFIRMED (the finding's "unbounded" is a paraphrase, but the code comment itself concedes late replies reach this branch).

Fixture gap: tests/test_connection.py:361-374 only pushes /ch/02/mix/fader and /ch/03/mix/on; fakedesk.py:53-55 docstring and _side_effects at fakedesk.py:1085-1086 confirm the FakeDesk applies goscene but never answers it, so the ack path is never exercised.

Reproduction: (1) the claimant's worktree test tests/integration/test_transport_assumptions.py::test_late_command_reply_is_not_a_parameter_update (worktree assumptions-transport-connection, which only adds an unrelated drop_next_inbound to fakedesk) FAILS on HEAD src: `assert ('/save', ('scene', 1)) not in [('/save', ('scene', 1))]`. (2) Feeding encode('/-action/goscene',0), encode('/load','scene',1), encode('/-action/clearsolo',0) to an unmodified X32Connection._handle_datagram yields on_update callbacks for all three, cache = {'/-action/goscene': 0, '/load': ('scene',1), '/-action/clearsolo': 0} and three 'update' events.

Impact check (why low is right, not higher): the only on_update subscriber is Desk._on_push (desk.py:232, 282-284) which looks the address up in the descriptor leaf/node index and no-ops for /save or /-action/*; X32Connection.get_cached has no caller in src/ (only tests), so the polluted connection cache is inert; the 'update' event reaches EventBus history and the dashboard log (webui.py:449-452 → webui/index.html:320-345 addEvent) as a bogus parameter-update row. No MCP tool reads event history. So the consequence is cosmetic/misleading logging plus a latent hazard if get_cached gains a caller — matching the claimant's own 'low'. No fallback was missed.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — Mechanism confirmed, consequence cosmetic, two supporting claims overstated.

CONFIRMED PART: connection.py:828-834 classifies every unmatched inbound message whose address starts with '/' and is not in _NOT_PARAMS={/info,/xinfo,/status,/} (connection.py:71) as a pushed parameter update: it is written to X32Connection._cache, dispatched to on_update callbacks and published as an 'update' event. Command-status replies are therefore misclassified when no waiter is pending: (a) recall_scene sends /-action/goscene via Desk._write -> conn.set() fire-and-forget (desk.py:1262, 871-884), so if the real desk acks '/-action/goscene ,i 0' (fx_routing_scenes.md §6.4/§13 item 10: UNCONFIRMED but best inference from DOC p.70-71) that ack ALWAYS lands in the update path; FakeDesk deliberately never answers goscene (fakedesk.py:53-55, _h at :1085) so the path is never exercised. (b) A /save (or /load,/delete,/rename,/copy) whose first reply arrives after the per-attempt timeout is re-sent by _request_bytes and the second ',si scene 1' reply has no waiter -> cached under '/save' and published as update. I ran the finder's worktree test (worktrees/assumptions-transport-connection tests/integration/test_transport_assumptions.py::test_late_command_reply_is_not_a_parameter_update, /-fake/latency 300) against its worktree: it FAILS today exactly as claimed (('/save',('scene',1)) in on_update stream; '/save' in conn._cache).

WHY IT DOES NOT BITE AT A GIG: I traced every consumer. (1) X32Connection.get_cached has zero callers in src/ (only definition at connection.py:581) — the polluted connection cache is dead state. (2) Desk._on_push (desk.py:282-283) only calls _invalidate_address, which is a no-op unless the address is a descriptor leaf/node; /-action/goscene IS a leaf (device.yaml:569-572) but it is a write-only trigger, so at worst a never-read section is dropped; '/save' is not a leaf -> no-op. Invalidation can only cause an extra re-read, never a wrong value. (3) EventBus subscribers: cfs.py:522 listens to connection.state only; desk.py:235 to 'write' only; webui.py:256/449 mirrors every event to the browser log, where index.html:310-327 renders one line 'update · /-action/goscene'. events.recent() has no product caller, no MCP tool surfaces events to the LLM. So the entire real-world effect is one dashboard log line — during a scene recall it is buried in the burst of hundreds of genuine /xremote pushes (fx_routing_scenes.md §6.2 'Every parameter that changed on recall is also pushed'). No tool reports wrong state, no wrong write, CFS untouched.

OVERSTATED PARTS: (i) 'transport.md §5.4: reply latency unbounded' misquotes the research — §5.4 says numeric latency is UNCONFIRMED but 'implies typical replies well under 10 ms on wired LAN' and recommends 50-100 ms timeouts; the code's per-attempt timeout is 500 ms (connection.py:245), and DOC fn.39-41 (§6.4) says /save/load status 'is returned' before the operation completes, so a >500 ms /save reply that triggers the retry is atypical, not expected. (ii) 'a stale fader value from a late GET reply is written into the connection cache with a fresh timestamp' is backwards: when a GET is retried, the FIRST (older) reply satisfies the second attempt's waiter and the unmatched one is the desk's LATER answer, i.e. the fresher value; caching it as 'desk is source of truth' (connection.py:831 comment, on_update docstring :624-625 'and unmatched replies') is a documented, deliberate and correct choice for parameter addresses — and moot anyway since nothing reads that cache. (iii) HANDOVER §4b: recall_scene/save_scene were never run on the real desk (show control was CUES), so the goscene-ack half remains inference, not an observed defect.

Net: a real classification gap (command-family replies should join _NOT_PARAMS or be filtered to descriptor-known parameter addresses) and a real FakeDesk fidelity gap (no goscene ack), but the only observable failure is cosmetic event-log noise. Severity low is correct; not medium because no tool lies and nothing fails spuriously.

## E101. [low] (transport-connection, confirmed) The desk coerces argument types: a ',i' sent to a float parameter (or ',f' to an int/enum) is converted numerically, so FakeDesk._coerce does float(int_arg) / int(round(float_arg)).

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:629-642 (t=='f': any int accepted as float) and :650-665 (t=='i': floats rounded); tests/test_connection.py:99-101 Responder stores whatever arrives; tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:57-85 never send a mistyped argument.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/osc.py encode(): a Python int → ',i', float → ',f' (HANDOVER §6 warns 'an int for a float param must be passed as float(x) or typetags="f"'); every conn.set(address, value) call site relies on the caller's Python type being right (desk._write via ParamSpec.to_raw returns floats today — verified for fader/pan/trim/eq gain/headamp — so this is latent, e.g. cfs.py:1338 needs an explicit typetags='f').

**Reality:** transport.md §1.1/§5.2: 'float parameters must be in range 0.0–1.0', int and float are distinct 4-byte big-endian encodings; the emulator's SET path (X32.c 2914-2980) switches on the RECEIVED tag and stores the raw 4 bytes into the value union, so ',i 1' on a fader stores the bit pattern 0x00000001 = 1.4e-45 as the float → fader at −∞ (desk behaviour UNCONFIRMED; at best it ignores the message, it does not convert).

**On a real desk:** A future call like conn.set('/bus/03/mix/fader', 1) or set('/fx/5/par/22', 0) (an int literal for 'unity'/'flat') passes every FakeDesk test and on the real desk either slams the bus to −∞ or is silently ignored while the tool reports success.

**Offline test:** Make FakeDesk strict: in _coerce, when spec.osc_type=='f' and the wire tag is 'i' store struct.unpack('>f', struct.pack('>i', v)) (emulator semantics) or ignore the SET; when osc_type=='i' and tag 'f', ignore. Then add a test that every product write path (Desk._write for each scale kind, cfs restore, provision) still round-trips — any int leaking to a float address now fails loudly.

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (low)** — Every citation checks out and the claimant did not miss a fallback — they correctly characterised the issue as a latent fake-fidelity gap rather than a live product defect.

1. FakeDesk really does numeric type coercion. src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:629-642 (`_coerce`, `t=="f"` branch) accepts any int/float and does `x = float(arg)`; :643-665 (`t=="i"` branch) does `v = int(round(arg))` for a float. The wire SET handler at fakedesk.py:1038-1044 calls `_coerce(a, spec, msg.args[0])` and never consults `msg.typetags`. Empirically (device.yaml loaded): a wire `,i 1` on /ch/01/mix/fader is stored as raw 1.0 (+10 dB), and `,f 0.7` on /ch/01/mix/on is stored as 1.

2. The unit-test Responder (tests/test_connection.py:99-101) stores `msg.args[0]` verbatim regardless of tag, and tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:57-85 only ever sends correctly-typed args (floats to faders/levels/eq/pan, ints/strings to on/color/enum) — no test exercises a mistyped SET.

3. Reality differs. I fetched the public emulator source (pmaillot/X32-Behringer X32.c, 5661 lines, same file transport.md cites) and read funct_params 2895-2980: the SET loop `switch (r_buf[f_len++])` on the RECEIVED tag; `case 'i'` writes `command[i].value.ii = endian.ii`, `case 'f'` writes `command[i].value.ff = endian.ff`, and `value` is a `union {int ii; float ff; char* str; void* dta;}` (X32.c 213-218). So `,i 1` on a float param stores bit pattern 0x00000001 → reads back as 1.4e-45 (≈ −∞ fader); no numeric conversion. transport.md §1.1 (line 31) only says 'float parameters must be in range 0.0–1.0' and grants type flexibility solely to enums/bools ('enum parameters can be sent as strings or integers'); §5.2 says nothing about int→float coercion; real-desk behaviour for a mistyped arg is not covered anywhere in docs/research (so it is unverified, as the claimant says). HANDOVER.md §6 (lines 224-225) explicitly warns 'an int for a float param must be passed as float(x) or typetags="f"' — i.e. the project itself believes the desk does NOT coerce, yet its FakeDesk does.

4. Product dependence is latent, exactly as claimed. I audited every write path: Desk._write/_write_value/_run_ramp/set_geq_band go through Scale.to_raw, whose level/lin/log/pan branches return floats via quantize()/_clamp01() (scales.py:73-75, 179-188 always yield float), and bool/enum/int branches return ints for `,i` params; meters.set_rta_source writes ints to /-prefs/rta/{source,pos,options,autogain,det} which device.yaml:560-565 declares `osc: i`; desk.py:1200/1203 write int 0 to mix/on (`,i`); server.py:1402 writes to chlink (`,i`); cfs.py:1338 defends explicitly with `float(...)` + `typetags="f"`; restore uses `/` text lines; no raw-OSC MCP tool exists (server.py tool list). So no current call sends a Python int to a float address — the FakeDesk leniency would only mask a future regression, which is why 'low' is the right severity.

Net: assumption real, encoded where cited, contradicted by the verified emulator semantics and by the project's own HANDOVER note, currently harmless in product code, offline test proposal (make _coerce tag-strict / emulator-faithful and assert all product write paths still round-trip) is sound. CONFIRMED at low.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — The fidelity gap is real but nothing depends on it, so it cannot bite at a gig today. (1) FakeDesk._coerce (src/x32mcp/fakedesk.py:629-665) does numerically convert a ',i' arriving at an 'f' leaf (float(arg)) and rounds a ',f' arriving at an 'i' leaf; the emulator SET path per transport.md §5.2 stores by the RECEIVED tag into a value union, and what a real desk does with a mismatched tag is UNCONFIRMED (research says neither 'converts' nor 'ignores') — so the fake is more forgiving than any source of truth warrants. That much is confirmed. (2) But the 'code depends on it' half fails. Every product write derives its wire arg from ParamSpec/Scale.to_raw: level/lin/log/pan return quantize(...)= int/int true division or db_to_fader/_clamp01 floats (scales.py:155-188, 402-424), enum/bool/int return ints. I loaded device.yaml and checked all 491 params: zero osc_type/scale-kind mismatches, and to_raw at boundary inputs (ints like -90, 0, 10, lo/hi, '-oo', -inf) never yields an int for an 'f' param nor a float for an 'i' param. All write sites (desk.py:879/940/1023/1040/1200/1236/1262/1369/1399/1431, server.py:1402/1480, meters.py:888-923, cfs.py:1338) send the correct Python type; cfs.py:1338 is already belt-and-braces (float(...) AND typetags='f'); restore uses conn.slash node text, which is type-free. No raw-OSC set tool is exposed to the LLM operator, so an agent cannot pass an int literal to a fader address. The author demonstrably knows the rule: HANDOVER §6, connection.set docstring (connection.py:520-524), and tests/test_connection.py:241 and :312-315 assert ',f' on the wire for fader writes. (3) The finding's own failure scenario is hypothetical ('a future call like conn.set(..., 1)') and it self-rates low/latent. The one plausible route to reality is that descriptor validation (descriptor.py:740-755) ties enum->'i' and str<->'s' but not 'f'->float-kind, so a future device.yaml entry with osc: f and an int scale would leak ',i' to a float leaf and FakeDesk would bless it. Worth the suggested hardening (make FakeDesk store int bits as float / ignore mismatched tags, and/or add a descriptor check that osc 'f' requires level|lin|log|pan), but as a real-desk defect it is theoretical: no tool lies and no wrong write occurs with the code as shipped.

## E102. [low] (transport-connection, partial) The desk is powered and reachable when the MCP server starts: X32_HOST autoconnect is attempted exactly once.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/server.py:185-190 (single connect attempt, failure is a log.warning); no test starts the server before the fake desk exists (integration fixtures always start FakeDesk first, tests/integration/conftest.py:30-48).

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/server.py:185-201; connection.py reconnect machinery (:909-954) only exists after one successful connect(), so a failed autoconnect leaves state DISCONNECTED with no retry; every tool then answers NOT_CONNECTED 'call connect(host) first' (server.py:224-234).

**Reality:** Operational common sense at a gig: the laptop (and Claude Desktop, which spawns the stdio server at launch) is up long before the desk finishes booting (~30-40 s) or while the stage box is still unpowered; HANDOVER §4a shows the desk can also reboot on a PSU fault.

**On a real desk:** Sound engineer opens the laptop, powers the rack, asks Claude to 'unmute the wedges' → NOT_CONNECTED although X32_HOST is configured; someone has to know to call connect('192.168.1.139') manually. Cosmetic-to-annoying, but it is the first interaction of every gig.

**Offline test:** Server-level test: start App with X32_HOST pointing at a port where FakeDesk is started 2 s later; assert connection_status becomes connected without a connect() tool call (autoconnect retried in the background with the reconnect backoff). Fails today.

> **Verifier 1: PARTIAL (low)** — Code citations check out: App.start() (src/x32mcp/server.py:185-190) makes exactly one autoconnect attempt and turns any failure into log.warning; X32Connection.connect() (connection.py:288-350) on an /info timeout tears the socket down, sets state DISCONNECTED and raises RequestTimeout (315-322) BEFORE the heartbeat/watchdog tasks are created (340-344), so the reconnect machinery (_watchdog_loop/_reconnect_loop, connection.py:909-954) never runs for a desk that was not up at launch; _desk() (server.py:224-234) then answers NOT_CONNECTED for every desk tool. No test exercises autoconnect at all (tests/integration/test_server_tools.py:36-42 forces x32_host=None; conftest.py:30-48 always starts FakeDesk before any connect), and HANDOVER §4a (line 133-134) does note the PSU-fault reboot. So the mechanism described is real and untested.

Why only PARTIAL: (1) this is not a hidden assumption the tests certified but an explicit, documented design decision — README.md:370-372 and :439 ('when set the server autoconnects at startup (a failure is logged, the server still starts)') and DESIGN.md:733-734 ('If X32_HOST is set, connect in lifespan (errors → logged, server still starts)') describe exactly this degradation path, with connect(host) as the intended recovery. (2) The claimant overstates the gig failure ('someone has to know to call connect(192.168.1.139) manually'): the failed autoconnect leaves conn._error = 'no /info reply from <host>:10023' (connection.py:320, preserved through _teardown 367-373 and surfaced by status.error 452-462), so every NOT_CONNECTED envelope reads '...call connect(host) first (last error: no /info reply from 192.168.1.139:10023)' (server.py:230-233, 725) — the configured IP is handed to the model in the error text, the server INSTRUCTIONS (server.py:109-110) tell it 'Call connect(host) first (discover_consoles finds desks on the LAN)', and discover_consoles (server.py:624-640) needs no connection. In practice Claude self-recovers with one extra tool call; nobody needs to know the IP. (3) The mid-gig reboot case the claimant leans on (HANDOVER §4a PSU fault) is already covered: §4a verified live that after a successful connect the connection degrades and 'reconnected by itself 16.7 s later after 4 probes with no connect() call'. Only the cold-start ordering (server before desk) lacks a retry. Net: accurate low-severity UX/robustness gap (no background autoconnect retry), correctly rated low by the claimant, but documented-by-design and better mitigated than the finding states; it sits at the edge of the brief's 'assumption baked into tests' class rather than squarely in it.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — Mechanics verified as stated: App.start() (src/x32mcp/server.py:185-190) makes exactly one connect() attempt for X32_HOST and logs a warning on failure; X32Connection.connect() (connection.py:288-322) leaves state DISCONNECTED on a missed /info, and the backoff/reconnect machinery (_watchdog_loop/_reconnect_loop, connection.py:909-954) is only started by a successful connect, so nothing retries in the background. Every tool then raises NOT_CONNECTED via _desk() (server.py:224-234).

But as a member of the brief's class ('a wrong belief about the world certified by tests that makes code misbehave') it is weak, and at a gig it barely bites:
1. It is a documented, deliberate design decision, not a hidden assumption: README.md:370-372 ('leave X32_HOST out and call connect(host) from the conversation — the server starts either way and only logs a warning when autoconnect fails'), README.md:439, DESIGN.md:733 ('If X32_HOST is set, connect in lifespan (errors → logged, server still starts)').
2. The failure is graceful and self-describing to the operator (Claude): connect timeout is 0.5 s x 3 = 1.5 s, well inside CONNECT_TIMEOUT_S=15 s, so _error is set to 'no /info reply from <host>:10023' and the NOT_CONNECTED envelope reads 'not connected to a desk: call connect(host) first (last error: no /info reply from 192.168.1.139:10023)' — it names both the remedy tool and the host. A connect(host, port) tool (server.py:643-662) and a discover tool exist, so 'unmute the wedges' costs Claude one extra tool call, not a human who 'has to know' the IP.
3. No tool lies and no wrong write happens: NOT_CONNECTED is the truth. The HANDOVER §4a PSU-reboot case is already covered once a session has connected (watchdog → DEGRADED → /info probes with repeating 8 s backoff → _recover).
So: accurate observation, reasonable robustness enhancement (background autoconnect retry), but cosmetic/already mitigated; severity low is the ceiling, and it is closer to a feature request than to an emulator-certified false belief.

## E103. [low] (transport-connection, confirmed) /xinfo is answered on the first try: connect() asks once with retries=0 and otherwise takes /info slot 2 as the console name.

**Encoded at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:328-335 (retries=0 for /xinfo; fallback name = /info slot 2); tests/test_connection.py:88-91 Responder always answers both; tests/integration/test_fakedesk.py:34-41.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:337-339 ConsoleInfo.name → server summaries (server.py:661,679,716,723), logs, dashboard identity; nothing re-queries later.

**Reality:** transport.md §3.1/§9 item 11: /info slot 2 is the constant 'osc-server' on every real desk (only the emulator puts the name there); §2: a single datagram can be lost. So one lost /xinfo reply names the desk 'osc-server' for the whole session.

**On a real desk:** connection_status: 'Connected to osc-server (X32RACK FW 4.13)'; with two desks (FOH + monitor world) the operator cannot tell from the tool which one Claude is driving. Cosmetic.

**Offline test:** fakedesk.drop_next(…) arranged so only the /xinfo reply is lost during connect (e.g. a drop_addresses fault), assert ConsoleInfo.name == 'X32-FAKE' (retry /xinfo like /info, or lazily re-query /-prefs/name). Fails today (name == 'osc-server').

> **Verifier 1: CONFIRMED (low)** — Both citations check out and there is no fallback the claimant missed. connection.py:318 sends /info with self._retries (default 2) but connection.py:330-335 sends /xinfo with retries=0 and, on RequestTimeout, keeps `name` = /info slot 2. transport.md §3.1 item 2 says /info server_name is "always osc-server on a real desk" (line 162; also line 194 "Do not key on slot 2"), §9 item 11 (line 643) repeats it, and §2 (Packet loss row, line 148) confirms plain UDP with silent loss. The FakeDesk itself already answers /info with "osc-server" (fakedesk.py:830), so the fallback yields "osc-server" even in the emulator once the single /xinfo datagram is lost. ConsoleInfo.name then flows into server.py:661, 679, 716, 723 (connect summary, status lines) and log line connection.py:346; nothing re-queries /xinfo or /-prefs/name later (the watchdog/reconnect path at connection.py:923 probes /info only). The module docstring (connection.py:19-21) documents 'sends /xinfo once ... falls back to the /info slot' as a deliberate decision, but that decision is exactly the wrong-world assumption: the fallback slot is a constant, not a name. Reproduced offline: in worktree wt/verify-xinfo-drop (commit b1f4120), tests/integration/test_xinfo_drop.py swaps fakedesk._handlers['/xinfo'] for a handler that drops only the first /xinfo request; connect() succeeds and c.status.console.name == 'osc-server' (test fails: 'osc-server' != 'X32-FAKE'). Impact is identity/cosmetic only (no wrong write, no CFS input), so severity low as claimed.

> **Verifier 2: PARTIAL (low)** — Mechanism is real: connect() sends /xinfo exactly once (src/x32mcp/connection.py:331, retries=0, 0.5 s) and on RequestTimeout keeps `name` from /info slot 2 (connection.py:326-335), which on a real desk is the constant "osc-server" (transport.md §3.1 line 162, §9 item 11 line 643). The FakeDesk itself is faithful here (fakedesk.py:829-834 answers /info with "osc-server" and /xinfo with the name), so this is not a fake-vs-desk mismatch; it is a network assumption (no datagram loss during the two-packet handshake) that no test violates — tests/test_connection.py:88-91 Responder and the FakeDesk fixture always answer /xinfo, and no test uses drop_next to lose only the /xinfo reply. Nothing re-queries the name later (ConsoleInfo built once at connection.py:337-339; reconnect loop only probes /info).

Why only PARTIAL/low: (1) it is a documented, deliberate decision (connection.py:19-21 "sends /xinfo once ... falls back to the /info slot"), not an unnoticed belief; (2) the consequence is purely cosmetic — no write, safety or CFS path keys on ConsoleInfo.name; (3) the 'two desks indistinguishable' claim is overstated: the same status strings print model and host:port (server.py:661 '... at {h}:{p}', 716 '... at {console.host}:{console.port}'), so FOH vs monitor desk remain distinguishable by IP/model; (4) probability at a gig is small — a single lost unicast UDP reply on a wired desk LAN at the one moment of connect (more plausible on venue Wi-Fi, still ~1%); (5) trivially recoverable by calling connect again. Worth a one-line fix (give /xinfo the same retries as /info, or treat 'osc-server' as 'unknown' and lazily read /-prefs/name), and the proposed offline test (drop only the /xinfo reply, assert name == 'X32-FAKE') would indeed fail today, but it would not actually bite anyone at a show.

## E104. [low] (transport-connection, partial) Whatever answers /info with four strings is a supported X32-family desk on tested firmware: connect() never compares console_model / console_version with descriptor.meta (model X32, firmware_tested '4.x').

**Encoded at:** tests/test_connection.py:88-89 and fakedesk.py:288-290 always report X32RACK/4.06/V2.07; src/x32mcp/connection.py:325-339 stores the strings without a check; device.yaml:47-50 meta has no accepted-models/min-firmware list.

**Code depends on it at:** src/x32mcp/connection.py:337-345 (CONNECTED unconditionally); downstream: meters.set_rta_source writes /-prefs/rta/autogain,/det (meters.py:911-925) and CFS relies on them; nodes parser tolerates FW 2.x token counts but nothing warns.
